articles.title: Joshua Gersen brings disciplined emotion to Lansing Symphony
articles.description: It would have been fun to report that the Lansing Symphony Orchestra, guest conductor Joshua Gersen and violinist Will Hagen crushed it Saturday night (Nov. 21). But they didn’t crush […]
articles.content: It would have been fun to report that the Lansing Symphony Orchestra, guest conductor Joshua Gersen and violinist Will Hagen crushed it Saturday night (Nov. 21). But they didn’t crush it. They cupped it, in their steady and strong hands, and gently breathed on it, as if it were a wayward warbler from the Arctic in search of warmth. Guest conductor Joshua Gersen and guest soloist Will Hagen gave Finnish composer Jean Sibelius’ violin concerto a tender, committed performance at Saturday’s Lansing Symphony Orchestra concert. Photo by Yotham Eshak “It” was indeed a visitor from the north, the fragile, sincere, nakedly confessional violin concerto of Finnish composer Jean Sibelius. Looking at Gersen, a no-nonsense conductor with an almost military bearing, and the youthful, bearded Hagen, raring to go and coiled with energy, you’d think a bit of a rumble was in the offing, but these two badass dudes and the orchestral home team weren’t here to flex their musical muscles. They gave the concerto a tender, committed performance of breathtaking delicacy. Gersen, the third of five guest conductors vying for the post of LSO music director, is not a charisma-driven maestro, but on Saturday night, he was the embodiment of musical precision and disciplined emotion. At every moment, from the most hushed to the most boisterous, he and the orchestra were saying something meaningful — to each other and to the audience. Everything Hagen did had an emotional underpinning, a reason for being there. If he stretched out a note, it wasn’t just to exhibit his velvety tone, but to penetrate the mystery of that note. If he double stopped, playing two notes at once, it wasn’t because he was showing off, but because two notes were needed to convey a mixed emotion or complex thought. After an ecstatic run up the scale, he would back off just a hair on the last note, as if to invite the orchestra to respond, making it clear that this concerto is a deep dialogue. Gersen discreetly managed the mercurial back and forth between soloist and orchestra with transparency and clarity. That dialogue took many forms, from full-on call and response between Hagen and the entire orchestra to tasty little exchanges with individual voices like principal bassoonist Michael Kroth. Hagen’s warm tone got about 15 degrees warmer in the slow movement, when every note carried an almost desperate emotional weight. It was almost a letdown when the finale rolled in, with its bouncy dum-ditty-dums. But after such a prolonged, heartfelt penetration into realms words can’t reach, there seemed little more to be said. Another sensitive, delicate performance opened Saturday’s concert. As a purely musical experience, Chris Rogerson’s “Noble Pond” is an absorbing tone poem, propelled by crosscurrents of bleak tragedy and lyrical beauty. Gersen and the orchestra took their time and gave the music a grand, even cosmic, sweep while letting each granular detail twinkle on the horizon. A backstory, provided in the concert notes and alluded to by Gersen in brief remarks before the concert, tells us that Rogerson wrote the music in response to a real-life news account of a 5-year-old boy who was killed by a stray bullet while fishing with his grandfather. You can’t un-know what you know. Music wrestles with tragedy all the time, but the specificity of this information made it hard to relax and accept whatever message the music could have conveyed. The boy’s death was a cruelly random and horrible accident. However earnest the intent, it made me queasy to see it co-opted as musical material for my comfortable contemplation. Gersen’s pre-concert comments on “overcoming adversity” didn’t connect the dots, either. Former New York Philharmonic assistant conductor Joshua Gersen is the third of five guest conductors leading the Lansing Symphony Orchestra this season to determine who will fill the shoes of departing music director Timothy Muffitt. Photo by Chris Lee The last work on Saturday’s slate, Beethoven’s famous Fifth Symphony, carried no such baggage. This music is about Beethoven’s struggles — with fate, with love, with deafness, with Napoleon, you name it. It’s his party, and he can rage if he wants to. As the da-da-da-doms of the famous first movement tumbled forth, things got slightly out of sync a couple of times, and there was a bit of juddering in the violins, but Gersen made sure the momentum never let up. After the prodigious energy of those four notes underwent fission into two notes, fusion into four again and was finally spent (at least in its purest form), a spacious sense of grandeur settled in for the rest of the ride. After the triumphant finale, Gersen did something I’ve never seen a conductor do. Instead of dispersing individual acknowledgments from the podium like a bride tossing out a bouquet, he waded deep into the wilds of the orchestra like a pith-helmeted ranger in the veldt and hunted down each contributing soloist and section, beginning with principal oboist Stephanie Shapiro, whom he practically lifted by the collar for public celebration. (Shapiro nailed that famous bit where a big orchestral buildup suddenly comes to a stop and the oboe is left to drip dry for about 45 seconds.) There was a lot to acknowledge, from the subsonic elephant rumbles of principal bassist Ed Fedewa and his crew to the defiant, elk-like blasts of the horns, who appear to be asking for the LSO to do a Wagner “Ring” cycle just so they can strut their stuff.

articles.title: What regional cannabis reform means for Michigan’s border goldmine
articles.description: For years, the economic engine powering a massive share of Michigan’s border dispensaries — and, by extension, the wholesale cultivators stretching across mid-Michigan — has been prohibition on the other side of […]
articles.content: For years, the economic engine powering a massive share of Michigan’s border dispensaries — and, by extension, the wholesale cultivators stretching across mid-Michigan — has been prohibition on the other side of our borders. From Menominee in the Upper Peninsula to the retail hubs dotting the Indiana and Ohio borders, Michigan operators have reaped the rewards as neighboring states have dragged their feet on adult-use reform. But with Ohio and Illinois having already legalized cannabis, incoming leadership in Wisconsin positioning legalization as a crucial fiscal tool to offset state budget and Medicaid funding gaps, and legislative rumblings stirring in Indiana, the writing is on the wall. The regional monopoly Michigan has enjoyed as the lone green oasis in the Midwest faces an expiration date. As Marijuana Moment recently reported, incoming Wisconsin lawmakers are no longer treating cannabis legalization as a distant cultural debate or a partisan talking point. Instead, they’re framing it as a desperate economic necessity to capture tax revenue currently bleeding out across their borders into Illinois and Michigan. When conservative states start viewing cannabis through the lens of fiscal survival rather than moral panic, reform accelerates rapidly. And then there’s the other Michigan border. While Ohio successfully launched its adult-use market, easing some of the pressure on our southern border, Indiana remains a fortress of prohibition. Yet political analysts note that as tax revenue pours into surrounding jurisdictions, even staunchly conservative lawmakers in Indianapolis are facing intense lobbying from agricultural and business groups eager not to miss out on the green wave. However, building a regulated market from scratch takes years of administrative buildup, licensing bottlenecks and municipal opt-out battles. Even if neighboring states pass legislation, Michigan still has a multi-year head start on cultivation infrastructure, processing sophistication and retail density. As Roy Liskey, co-owner of Laingsburg dispensary Local Roots, told City Pulse, “We aren’t worried about Ohio or Wisconsin opening tomorrow. Building out a supply chain takes years of bureaucratic heavy lifting. Our advantage right now isn’t just geography, it’s that our craft operators have spent years dialing in quality while everyone else was arguing in statehouses.” Midwest legalization is not a crisis to panic over; it’s a definitive timeline for market maturation. Far from spelling doom for Michigan’s cannabis market, a fully legalized Midwest should serve as a long overdue wake up call for our in-state operators. For years, Michigan has suffered from substantial overproduction and brutal price compression, largely because our production capacity vastly outstrips in-state consumer demand. While out-of-state consumers have helped absorb excess biomass, true economic stability will only arrive when federal interstate commerce laws allow Michigan’s top-tier craft cultivators to legally export their products across state lines to underserved markets nationwide. When neighboring states finally come online, the operators who survive won’t be the ones sitting on the border, hoping for drive-by traffic from out-of-state plates. They’ll be the ones with ironclad brand loyalty, superior product quality and distribution networks that stretch across the state, from Grand Rapids and Lansing down to Detroit. If you’re a cultivator relying on border-town stores to move volume, or a retailer padding your monthly sales numbers with out-of-state tourists, now is the time to audit your brand equity. When consumers in Wisconsin, Indiana and beyond no longer have to drive across state lines just to buy clean live resin or premium pre-rolls, your product needs to be good enough that they miss it when it’s gone. The borders won’t stay closed forever. The question for Michigan’s retailers and cultivators alike is simple: Will you be ready when the rest of the country catches up? Chris Silva writes the Lansterdam column for City Pulse and serves as a columnist and editor for MiCannaPress. Have a tip? Reach out at chris@gomicannapros.com.

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asks court to delay firing-squad execution so he can fight sentence
articles.description: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asks court to delay firing-squad execution so he can fight sentence AP News Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asks court to halt his execution ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Fort Hood shooter asks court to delay execution scheduled for next week The Washington Post ACLU asks court to halt first military execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan KSAT Fort Hood mass sho
articles.content: KILLEEN, Texas (AP) — Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in an attack at the Texas military base in 2009, asked a federal court Tuesday to delay his execution by firing squad so he can prepare a petition contesting his sentence. In the filing, which Hasan signed, he says he “intends to demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his resulting sentence of death were obtained and are maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights.” Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, was found guilty of multiple counts of murder as well as attempted murder for the more than 30 people wounded by gunfire in the attack. The court filing has the potential to add major delays to the Trump administration’s plans for the execution, which had been scheduled for next week, while the legal battle plays out. A hearing has been set for Wednesday morning. Following an order from President Donald Trump, Army and Pentagon officials in October announced the military execution, the first since 1961 and the first by firing squad since World War II. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth then declared that the execution would be livestreamed, sparking outcry before Trump later pulled the plug on that plan. One of Hasan’s main arguments would be that he was denied the ability to present the argument that his actions were legally justifiable, “because he was defending the Afghan Taliban, who are trying to establish Islam as Supreme Law of their land, from an unlawful attack by the United States Army — in short, ‘defense of others,’” according to court documents. After the judge in his 2013 trial forbid Hasan, who relieved his lawyers and presented his own defense, from making that argument to the jury, Hasan largely sat silent throughout the three-week trial. As a result, while the military called nearly 90 witnesses, Hasan rested his case without calling a single person to testify in his defense and made no closing argument. The move convinced his court-appointed standby lawyers that Hasan’s only goal was to get a death sentence. Tuesday’s filing says Hasan intends to keep representing himself as he fights the execution, though he is being assisted by lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union Capital Punishment Project. The ACLU lawyer listed for Hasan in court records and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Hasan’s case has been assigned to Judge Tony Mattivi in U.S. District Court in Kansas, court records show. It was filed there because Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. Mattivi was nominated by Trump to serve as a federal judge and was just confirmed by the Senate on June 9. According to his judicial biography, from 2009 to 2013, Mattivi was the lead prosecutor in the capital military commission at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, against the al-Qaida operative who masterminded the bombing of the USS Cole. The court action came during uncertainty over some of the logistics of the execution that had been scheduled for Dec. 3. Military officials said Tuesday that three survivors of the shooting at Fort Hood would not be allowed to witness it. On Nov. 10, the Army said that three survivors could not attend because none of them was the direct victim of those charges, citing regulations governing military executions. An email sent Tuesday and shared with The Associated Press by recipients said military officials rejected their request for reconsideration, citing security and space issues. The three argued that the Army should apply a broader definition of “victim” from the Uniform Code of Military Justice that says a victim can be someone who suffered “direct physical, emotional or pecuniary harm.” They argued that the military’s refusal to allow them to attend was saying they had not been victims because they were not struck by bullets. The letter signed by the commandant of Fort Leavenworth said the three cannot appeal again. “Please understand that this is not meant as a judgment on any emotional injury you or others suffered as a result of CP Hasan’s crimes,” it said. Retired Col. Kathy Platoni, who would have been Hasan’s supervisor during a planned deployment to Afghanistan, said the denial felt like a betrayal. “I would desperately like to attend,” Platoni said from her home in Ohio. “To look Hasan in the eye and say, ‘You didn’t get me.’” The Army said in a statement that regulations specify who can witness a military execution and reiterated the size and space restrictions. Platoni said the survivors from her unit deployed to Afghanistan 29 days after the attack, because, “we still served our country, and if we didn’t, (Hasan) would have won.” She said the building where Hasan initially opened fire had been crowded with returning soldiers and those preparing to deploy. She had been moved to another building when the attack began. “The looks on the faces of my friends and colleagues as they carried in the dying and wounded that day ... it will haunt me for the rest of my life,” she said. She said they carried in the badly wounded captain who had rushed Hasan with a chair to try to stop the shooting. “I was throwing computers to the ground trying to get the tablecloths because we needed blankets. We didn’t have medical supplies or even water,” she said. “I still have that blood-stained uniform, from kneeling down next to that young man, trying to get him to stay with us. That will be with me forever.” Julia Wilson, who was nine months pregnant when Hasan opened fire, said her witness request was also denied and that the way the military has handled the case caused her anguish. “We have faced institutional betrayal after institutional betrayal,” Wilson said. “We remain on that battlefield because of that ... if they don’t fix it, we’re never going to leave that battlefield. We’ll never heal.” Platoni said she did not think space was really the issue. The military told victims and survivors that about 160 witnesses would be allowed to attend the execution, and through her work with survivors and families of victims, she believed about 90 people had decided to go. Platoni conceded that those details may have changed. Retired Maj. C. Alan Hopewell testified at Hasan’s trial. He confirmed Hasan’s identity after he was shot by two service members attempting to halt his rampage. One of those officers had asked Hopewell to accompany her to the execution. “I’m disappointed that our status as victims is not recognized,” Hopewell said Tuesday. “A bullet missed me and hit my car. I guess if the bullet had hit me … they would consider me a victim and let me attend.” Hopewell, Platoni and Wilson said they will continue to push for the Fort Hood shooting to be redefined as an act of domestic terrorism instead of workplace violence. Of attending the execution, “I guess it feels more like a duty, like a fulfillment of my responsibility to those soldiers who were killed and injured, who were threatened,” Hopewell said. Lauer reported from Philadelphia, and Toropin from Washington.

Martha Ford, former Lions owner with link to auto giants, dies at 101
articles.description: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford has died. She was 101. The Lions say she died Tuesday at her home, surrounded by family.
articles.content: FILE - Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford is seen during pregame of an NFL football game against the Buffalo Bills, Nov. 24, 2022, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, File)(Paul Sancya/AP Photo/Paul Sancya / AP)Martha Firestone Ford, the tire heiress who became a link between two of the automotive industry's most iconic families and later took over the NFL's Detroit Lions, has died. She was 101.The Lions say she died Tuesday at her home in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, surrounded by family. No cause of death was given.Ford was a granddaughter of tire magnate Harvey Firestone, and her husband, William Clay Ford Sr., was Henry Ford's grandson. He also owned the Lions for a half-century before his death in 2014.Martha Ford then took over his controlling interest in the team, keeping it within the family. Although she seldom spoke to reporters or commented publicly on the direction of the franchise, her influence was felt. She was in charge of the team from 2014 until 2020, when she turned the Lions over to her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp.The Lions made the playoffs in 2014, but lost seven of their first eight games the following season. In November 2015, the team fired its president and general manager in a midseason shakeup. When she announced the changes, Ford told fans the franchise intended to “identify and hire the very best leadership in order to produce a consistently, winning football team.”The Lions played better down the stretch that season, and after hiring Bob Quinn as their new general manager, they returned to the playoffs a year later.“Martha was special," NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said in a statement. "She cared so deeply about her family, the players, their fans, and the city of Detroit. She was committed to making the Lions - and the game of football - better. Martha and her husband, William Clay Ford, led the franchise with dignity and integrity. We will miss her kindness and sweet sense of humor. We extend our deepest condolences to her children, the entire Ford family, and the Lions’ organization.”Born Sept. 16, 1925, in Akron, Ohio, Martha Parke Firestone graduated from Vassar College in 1946 and married William Clay Ford the next year.Their wedding received a huge amount of coverage - looking back in 2014, the Akron Beacon Journal described it as “Akron’s royal wedding” - and the marriage joined two families that already had a long history.Harvey Firestone, the founder of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Co., was a close friend of Ford Motor Co. founder Henry Ford. Ford chose Firestone to supply the tires for the first Model T in 1906. The two men often went on long camping trips together, sometimes accompanied by their friend Thomas Edison.Martha and William Clay Ford had three daughters and a son. Their son, William Clay Ford Jr., is the current executive chairman of Ford Motor Co. In 2001, Bridgestone/Firestone and Ford severed their nearly 100-year relationship because of a dispute over a series of deadly tire failures on the Ford Explorer.Sheila Ford Hamp is the Lions’ principal owner and chairman.William Clay Ford’s first full season leading the Lions was in 1964, seven years after they won an NFL title. Since that 1957 championship, the franchise has won playoff games in 1992 and 2023 and has not played in the Super Bowl.Although Martha Ford kept a low profile, the shakeup in the middle of the 2015 season was a sign that she was more than willing to bring about change in an effort to reverse the team’s fortunes. Then-coach Jim Caldwell said she was very much a presence within the organization.“I think visible ownership is great, and Mrs. Ford does it extremely well,” Caldwell said in 2015. “She’s there before games and she’s there after games, and I think guys enjoy that part of it. She comes to practice and things of that nature, so it’s been fun.”Even at 101, she attended games, including a win over the Minnesota Vikings earlier this month.Martha Ford also made an impact in the Detroit community. She was an officer on the board for Detroit Lions Charities and on the board of the Henry Ford Health System. Martha and William Clay Ford were credited with helping establish the Maplegrove Center, a substance abuse treatment facility in West Bloomfield.In 2017, Forbes estimated Martha Ford’s net worth at more than $1.4 billion. She is survived by her four children, 14 grandchildren, and 17 great-grandchildren.

articles.title: Supporters look to next year for 'Right to Sit' legislation
articles.description: Some Michigan workers' advocates are hoping to pass a “right to sit” law in the state. The policy would require employers to give workers a reasonable chance to sit.
articles.content: Johnnie Mae Cullins, right, says she was fired after being unable to return to work while her employer refused chair accommodations despite a note from her doctor.(Colin Jackson / Michigan Public Radio Network )Some workers' advocates and Michigan lawmakers are standing up for “right to sit” legislation.A Michigan bill would require employers to give workers a reasonable spot to sit while on the job. Violators would face a $250 fine per affected employee, multiplied by each two-week period the law isn’t followed.The Democrat-backed proposal is stalled in committee in the Republican-led Michigan House of Representatives. Democrats take majority control of the full state Legislature next year.Lead sponsor, state Rep. Dylan Wegela (D-Garden City), said this should be a “no-brainer” for lawmakers to pass if they’re going to be pro-worker.“There’s no reason to not provide seats for jobs that can be done while seated. There’s no logical explanation from corporations to deny that ability, and it also should be protected by state law. We should be demanding that we have these basic rights at work,” Wegela said during a news conference in Highland Park Tuesday.Supporters of the legislation argued it would help protect workers' dignity when employers don’t provide adequate disability accommodations.One woman at Tuesday’s event said she lost her job as an ID checker at a casino when her old employer wouldn’t honor a doctor’s note meant to limit how much she was standing.Johnnie Mae Cullins originally worked in casino security but was moved to the ID-checker position after a knee replacement caused her to fail a physical test.The shift came with a pay cut and the casino argued it didn’t need to provide a chair since the new position was enough of an accommodation. Meanwhile, Cullins said she had other life stresses like helping her blind adult son get to independent living classes.Cullins said she fell into extreme depression and was placed on medical leave.Cullins said she was fired after being unable to return while her employer still refused chair accommodations. It was a hard transition after being at her job for so long.“When you’re somewhere that long working and then you’re not working no more, it feels like, what am I going to do? You know, because you’re used to working,” Cullins said.Cullins unsuccessfully sued for employment discrimination.As laid out in a Michigan Court of Appeals ruling, the trial court accepted her old employers’ argument that the disability limited her ability to do key parts of her job.“The trial court also reasoned that, to the extent plaintiff’s failure-to-accommodate claim was premised on defendant’s failure to provide plaintiff with a chair, the claim had to be dismissed because plaintiff failed to provide any evidence tending to establish that she asked defendant for a chair in a written request, which the court opined was required to sustain a failure-to-accommodate claim,” the appellate court opinion read.Attorney Rick Martin represents Cullins in her lawsuit, which she is appealing to the Michigan Supreme Court. He took the lower court decisions to mean the case got thrown out because the doctor’s note said she needed to sit for long periods rather than explicitly saying she needed a “chair.”Martin worries the rulings set an informal precedent that could make disability protections contingent on using exactly the right words.“If you don’t use magic words, the employer[s] are still able to discriminate and retaliate against injured workers and disabled workers,” Martin said.

Michigan gets 2028 Democratic primary debate
articles.description: Michigan will host one of 12 debates between Democratic presidential hopefuls in the 2028 election cycle.
articles.content: Curtis Hertel Jr. was selected as chair of the Michigan Democratic Party during its spring convention in February 2025.(Rick Pluta / MPRN)Michigan will host one of 12 debates between Democratic presidential hopefuls in the 2028 election cycle.The Democratic National Committee made the announcement this week when it released its framework for the next election cycle.Michigan’s presidential primary will be on February 22, 2028. It’ll be the fifth Democratic primary after South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, and New Mexico. With the exception of a 10-day gap between the first two, all are a week apart.Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel advocated for giving the state a larger role in the primary process.“I think that Michigan looks like America,” Hertel said. “We're the most diverse battleground state in the country … racially, economically, geographically.”Hertel said he prefers a national popular vote so candidates have to campaign everywhere, but until things change, Michigan is a good early test for presidential hopefuls.“I don't like the Electoral College. I hope it's someday that it's not the major deciding point for all this,” Hertel said. But as long as we have it, we know that Michigan is going to be a key state, and those organizing dollars should be spent in those states early.”The DNC has placed some restrictions on who qualifies for debates. If the field is large, two debates of up to 10 participants each would take place.Participating candidates must also sign a pledge that they will not use Super PAC money against fellow Democrats during the primary process.A date and place have not yet been set for Michigan’s debate.

Tonya Burns sworn in as Flint's new mayor, vows she will address city's gun violence
articles.description: Mayor-elect Tonya Burns pledged to deal with Flint's violent crime problem.
articles.content: Flint mayor-elect Tonya Burns [right] takes her oath of office. She officially takes over the mayor's office December First. (Steve Carmody / Michigan Public )Flint’s incoming mayor is pledging to deal with the city’s violent crime problem.Tonya Burns was sworn in Tuesday.Speaking to an overflow crowd at Flint City Hall, Burns focused on gun violence.“It is not OK for us to hear gunshots every day. It’s not OK that we hit the floor,” said Burns, “It’s not OK when I take calls from seniors who sleep in their basements because they’re scared to sleep in their bedrooms because of stray bullets.” The Flint police department has said the number of violent crimes reported in the city is down slightly so far this year, though the number of homicides is up slightly compared to this time last year. Burns officially takes over Flint’s mayor’s office December 1. The former city council member defeated incumbent mayor Sheldon Neeley in this month’s election. The two often clashed during the past few years.

Trump says he’ll meet with El-Sayed to discuss ‘Trumpcare’
articles.content: Note: AI technology was used to generate this article’s audio. US President Donald Trump has said he plans to meet with Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss a proposal for universal healthcare, expressing openness to a potential compromise over the progressive lawmaker's plan to rebrand “Medicare for All” as “Trumpcare.” In an interview with The New York Post published on Nov. 24, Trump praised El-Sayed's proposal to put his name on a universal healthcare programme, describing the idea as “very smart” and saying the incoming Michigan senator had done “a very good job.” “I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump told the newspaper, without providing a date for the meeting. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” Trump also expressed optimism about the possibility of reaching agreements with Democrats on healthcare and other legislation, saying the two sides could accomplish “great things together.” “I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point I think they’re going to want to negotiate,” he said. “I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together.” El-Sayed, who has also expressed willingness to meet with Trump, previously floated the idea of naming his proposed universal healthcare programme after the president in an effort to secure his support. Earlier this month, the Democratic senator-elect shared a mock-up of a golden healthcare insurance card bearing Trump's name, tagging the president and writing: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee health care for every American, from cradle to grave.” Speaking to NPR, El-Sayed said he was willing to put Trump's name on the programme if that helped secure its passage. “Put his name on it,” he said. “He’ll probably pass it. I’m not above doing that. I don’t care what it’s called.” El-Sayed also directly invited Trump to discuss areas of potential cooperation, saying: “Donald, if you’re listening, there’s a lot we could work on. Happy to have a meeting. Let’s figure out what we can work on and get done.” The proposed outreach marks a notable shift in tone between the two politicians following a hostile election campaign. Trump previously described El-Sayed as a “jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you,” while El-Sayed accused the president of using hateful rhetoric. In his victory speech, El-Sayed said Michigan voters had rejected what he characterised as a campaign focused on his identity rather than policy issues. “Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” he said. The proposal comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, giving the party an opportunity to advance its legislative priorities. However, “Medicare for All,” which would establish a single-payer healthcare system, has long faced opposition from Republicans. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that such a system could increase federal healthcare subsidies from $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion by 2030, although patients' overall out-of-pocket healthcare costs would decline. A September poll by the Kaiser Family Foundation found that 66% of US adults supported a single government health plan, including 84% of Democrats and 34% of Republicans. Trump also told The New York Post that he expected to meet regularly with Democratic leaders, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, expressing hope that cooperation between the parties would lead to legislative agreements. “We’ll probably end up meeting quite a bit,” he said, adding that Americans should hope the two sides “get along because we can do a lot of great things together.” Trump said healthcare reform was among the areas where cooperation could be possible, arguing that the existing Affordable Care Act, commonly known as Obamacare, had failed. “Obamacare hasn’t worked, and I’d love to get great health care for the people of our country,” he told the newspaper. articles.title: Trump calls El-Sayed ‘smart guy’ and says he’ll meet with him about ‘Trumpcare’
articles.content: President Donald Trump said Tuesday he plans to meet with Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss the Democrat’s “Medicare for All” proposal, which El-Sayed has pitched to rebrand as “Trumpcare.” “He’s a smart guy,” Trump told the New York Post in a 45-minute interview in the Oval Office of El-Sayed’s suggestion to rename the plan after him. “He did a good job. He actually did a very good job.” “I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump continued. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” El-Sayed made universal health care central to his pitch on the campaign trail, where he and Trump were constantly at odds. But earlier this month, he posted an image of a gold “Trumpcare” card on X, calling upon the president to guarantee healthcare “from cradle to grave.” In an unexpected move, Trump on Saturday reposted a screenshot of the post. CNN has reached out to El-Sayed for comment. According to the Post, Trump on Tuesday called the pitch to attach his name to the universal health care proposal “very smart.” Trump also said he and the newly elected Democratic majorities in Congress could do “great things together,” though he warned things might start off confrontationally. “I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point I think they’re going to want to negotiate. I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together,” Trump said. The president’s comments mark a sharp turnaround from the midterm campaign, when he and the then-Democratic nominee traded bitter political and personal attacks. At a rally in October, Trump referred to El-Sayed, who will be the country’s first Muslim senator, as “Mohammed” and falsely declared that the former public health official is a “jihadist.” Days before the election, Trump urged voters at a Florida rally to “send him back to where he came from,” despite El-Sayed being born and raised in Michigan. “If he won, that’d be a devastating blow for our country,” Trump said at another campaign stop during the cycle. El-Sayed, in turn, was a frequent critic of the Trump administration, railing against the president and Vice President JD Vance on the campaign trail. “They can keep saying my name,” he said in the closing days of his race. “They can keep pointing to my faith. My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.” But in the wake of a blue wave that will give Democrats control of both the House and Senate for Trump’s final two years in power, both sides are showing openness to discussion. Earlier this month, El-Sayed signaled that he’d be willing to meet with Trump or anyone else, regardless of party, to help advance his goals in the Senate. “I’ve never met the man. He is the president of the United States. I am the US senator-elect from the state of Michigan. I am happy to meet with him, like I’ll meet with anyone who can advance the goals I ran on to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for all,” El-Sayed said on ABC’s “This Week.” Vance’s office said last week that it had begun reaching out to the incoming senator after hearing the Michigan Democrat wanted a meeting.

articles.title: Tennessee newspaper says its new owner will be a local resident: Al Gore, the former vice president
articles.description: Tennessee newspaper says its new owner will be a local resident: Al Gore, the former vice president AP News Former U.S. Vice President Al Gore to buy Tennessee newspaper The Tennessean Former VP Al Gore returning to his roots to become new owner of Tennessee newsaper NBC News ‘Carthage Resident Al Gore’ Buys His Hometown Tennessee Newspaper The New York Times Al Gore to purchase his hometown newspaper The Washington
articles.content: Former Vice President Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a newspaper owner in his Tennessee town. The Lake family, which has operated the Carthage Courier for five decades, said Tuesday it will sell the paper to Gore in the coming weeks. The weekly paper serves Smith County in central Tennessee, which has roughly 20,000 residents and sits about 55 miles (88 kilometers) east of Nashville. As the beleaguered news industry struggles with newspaper closures and growing news deserts, Gore characterized the purchase as a move that preserves an independent local voice in Carthage and Smith County. “Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the (Nashville) Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community,” Gore said in a statement. Terms of the sale weren’t disclosed, and it wasn’t clear how involved Gore, 78, will be in the paper’s operations. His office and the outlet wouldn’t answer questions Tuesday or provide additional details. The Courier’s announcement omitted Gore’s political resume, presenting him simply as a local man buying his small town’s paper to keep it locally owned. Before entering politics, Gore spent six months as a military reporter in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam War. He returned to Tennessee and worked for a few years as an investigative reporter at The Tennessean before running for Congress in 1976. Gore, a Democrat, represented Tennessee in both chambers of Congress, served as President Bill Clinton’s vice president from 1993 to 2001, and ran for president twice. After losing the 2000 presidential election to George W. Bush, he went on to win the Nobel Peace Prize for his climate activism and an Academy Award for the documentary, “An Inconvenient Truth.” The Courier’s website notes that it covered the early political pursuits of Gore’s father, Albert Gore Sr., who represented the state in the U.S. House and Senate. Tim Franklin, chair of local news at Northwestern University’s Medill School of Journalism, Media, Integrated Marketing Communications, said Carthage residents may have “some healthy skepticism” about a politician owning the paper. “But I would be surprised if the Carthage Courier becomes a mouthpiece for the Democratic Party,” he said. Franklin wondered if the former vice president might write a column, and if the publication would remain narrowly focused on local news. Gore is far from the first politician to purchase or own a newspaper. Throughout the 1900s, several senators, governors and even a U.S. president, Warren Harding, had local papers in their business portfolios. More recently, consumer advocate Ralph Nader, one of Gore’s former political rivals, helped launch a local newspaper in Winsted, Connecticut, in 2023 that was purchased months later by a national media company. Associated Press journalist Mike Sisak contributed to this report.

articles.title: After years of controversy, Detroit zoning change will limit concrete plant’s footprint
articles.description: The council’s decision comes after a contentious public hearing where residents, State Sen. Stephanie Chang and others spoke out against the operation, saying it creates dust and noise. But advocates, including staff of the plant, touted dust mitigation efforts and concern for their jobs.
articles.content: Detroit City Council signed off on zoning changes that will prevent a controversial concrete mixing facility from further expanding in the Cadillac Heights neighborhood. The rezoning measure, approved Tuesday by a 7-2 vote, will restrict industrial activity at the site of Kronos concrete and surrounding area. The current facility can stay and operate as normal. City Council President James Tate and Pro Tem Coleman A. Young II as well as members Scott Benson, Gabriela Santiago-Romero, Denzel Anton McCampbell, Renata Miller and Latisha Johnson voted for the measures. Council Members Angela Whitfield-Calloway and Mary Waters — who proposed a failed motion to postpone the vote — voted no. The council’s decision comes after a contentious public hearing late last week where residents, State Sen. Stephanie Chang and others spoke out against the operation, saying it creates dust and noise and other negative quality of life impacts for neighbors. But advocates, including union members, staff of the plant and workers of another area concrete facility touted dust mitigation efforts and other investments as well as concern for their jobs. The rezoning approval is the latest development for the site following a BridgeDetroit and ProPublica investigation that revealed how city officials helped Crown Enterprises, a real estate company owned by Detroit’s wealthy Moroun family, obtain property in the east side community and then provided latitude when its Kronos facility violated environmental laws. Waters said ahead of the vote that she had a list of questions Monday that had yet to be answered, and could not “be supportive” of downzoning until they were. Whitfield-Calloway did not say during the session why she voted no. Billionaire businessman Matthew Moroun, who owns Crown, appeared before the council and urged members to vote no, saying the land impacted by the zoning change did not have any commitments that the downsizing was unfair, given how Crown obtained the parcels as part of a land swap with the city. Over the last seven years, Crown has obtained dozens of parcels in Cadillac Heights — some through a land deal with the city in 2019 and others after residents sold their parcels and left. In all, the company now owns more than 160 lots in the neighborhood, most of which are barren. “I’ve invested millions,” Moroun said. “I believe that this is a question of fairness and integrity.” Moroun said between the air quality monitors at the Kronos site — which he claims have never violated air quality requirements — and the continued compliance with thrice weekly inspections from the city’s Buildings, Safety Engineering, and Environmental Department (BSEED). Residents have filed about 80 complaints to both city and state environmental offices related to the Kronos site, according to records obtained by BridgeDetroit and ProPublica. The city has issued several tickets to Kronos for violating Detroit’s fugitive dust ordinance, passed in 2024 to limit pollution. The law requires businesses such as concrete plants and scrapyards to submit plans to limit dust and prevent it from spreading into neighborhoods. On Oct. 7, the city received a complaint about Kronos and an inspector found the company had spread dust in the neighborhood and had piles of materials that should have been blocked from view, city spokesperson Georgette Johnson recently said. Kronos wrote in a letter to the city that it swept and watered the streets and reduced the height of the piles. Johnson confirmed that Crown did correct the problems. On Tuesday, a few residents provided public comment, expressing a mix of feelings about the zoning proposal. One caller told the council that leadership is “expected to vote for quality of life” and protect residents from harm and the proposal aimed to do that. At least two speakers with a youth skilled trades organization for Black men spoke against the downzoning, with one member stating the group stands for, “choosing drills and hammers over weapons and creating opportunities instead of taking them away.” “I believe in … investing in neighborhood jobs, and investing in our future. As residents, we deserve both a healthy community and a strong economy,” said group member Juan Jones. Attorney Melvin Butch Hollowell, who represents Crown, pushed back against criticism during Tuesday’s meeting and the recent public hearing, arguing that, “There is no science indicating environmental problems at or near the Kronos site.” Hollowell maintained during public comment that the rezoning matter is “a jobs killer with no environmental upside that violates the terms of the land swap agreement that was approved by the City Council.” In mid-September and in October, Crown’s attorneys threatened legal action if city officials changed the zoning. They contend that doing so would devalue the property and create uncertainty about future development. BridgeDetroit did not receive an immediate answer Tuesday about whether Crown’s attorneys would be following through with legal action following the vote. The zoning amendment, which was sent to the council from the City Planning Commission, permits heavy to light industrial, which will allow buildings such as warehouses but excludes facilities like concrete plants. The commission also recommended that other lots be zoned for residential and commercial purposes. Kenneth Dobson, a Crown spokesman, previously told BridgeDetroit and ProPublica in October that if the zoning changes, the company would not make promised improvements, including new landscaping and sidewalks. He said the improvements would not be allowed under the new zoning and that they also wouldn’t be a sound business decision. City planning staff, however, has said the company can still make the improvements. Dobson did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday afternoon. BridgeDetroit reporter Jena Brooker contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump vows to meet with Abdul El-Sayed on golden ‘Trumpcare,’ tells The Post he and Dems could do ‘great things’
articles.content: See more of our coverage in your search results. WASHINGTON — President Trump will meet with Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss passing the “Medicare for All” plan as “Trumpcare,” he told The Post, saying he and Democrats could do “great things together.” Trump praised the Michigan Democrat’s branding of his single-payer plan with the Trump name as “very smart” in an Oval Office interview and sounded optimistic they could come to an agreement. “He’s a smart guy,” Trump said, chuckling when The Post asked him about the golden “Trumpcare” plan the lefty Dem has been promoting during a 45-minute interview in the Oval Office on Tuesday. “He did a good job. He actually did a very good job.” “I know I’ll be meeting with him,” he added, without specifying the date. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” The president expressed confidence that he and Democrats could make legislative deals, adding the two sides could do “great things together.” “I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point I think they’re going to want to negotiate. I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together.” El-Sayed’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment but the senator-elect has expressed a willingness to sit down with the president. “Donald, if you’re listening, there’s a lot we could work on,” El-Sayed told NPR earlier this month. “Happy to have a meeting. Let’s figure out what we can work on and get done.” The incoming Michigan Democrat dangled the idea of a golden insurance card providing universal health care and embossed with the name “Trumpcare” — an obvious move to court the president’s support. Posting a mockup of the card on social media, he tagged the president in the post and wrote: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee health care for every American, from cradle to grave.” He would do whatever it takes to pass the plan, El-Sayed said, adding he doesn’t care what it’s called. “Put his name on it,” he told NPR. “He’ll probably pass it. I’m not above doing that. I don’t care what it’s called.” This is a message for @realDonaldTrump. Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave. pic.twitter.com/f32IYs3FXG It’s a change in tenor from both men since the midterm election. On the campaign trail, Trump referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you” while El-Sayed accused him of “hateful” rhetoric and praised Michigan voters for ignoring it. In his victory speech, El-Sayed noted: “Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face.” Democrats will control the House and Senate come January and “Medicare for All” has long been a dream of the progressive wing of the party. Republicans, however, abhor the plan. A single-payer option would cause government costs to skyrocket. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that it would increase federal subsidies for health care from $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion by 2030. However, the total out-of-pocket costs for patients would decline. For it to become law, however, Trump would have to agree to sign, instead of veto, any legislation. A Kaiser Family Foundation poll in September found that 66% of adults favor a single government health plan but 84% of those are Democrats and only 34% are Republicans. articles.title: Georgia's Fulton County ordered to give copy of 2020 election records seized by FBI to state board
articles.description: Georgia's Fulton County ordered to give copy of 2020 election records seized by FBI to state board AP News Judge orders Fulton County to give 2020 records to State Election Board The Atlanta Journal-Constitution Fulton County ordered to turn over copies of 2020 ballots The Hill F.B.I. Is Still Looking for Evidence That Georgia’s 2020 Election Was Rigged The New York Times Judge orders Georgia’s Fulton County to turn
articles.content: ATLANTA (AP) — A judge on Tuesday ordered Georgia’s Fulton County to turn over a digital copy of ballots and other election records seized by the FBI earlier this year to the State Election Board, which had been trying for more than two years to obtain certain records from the 2020 election in the state’s most populous county. Fulton County Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe ordered that the records be delivered to the state board by 5 p.m. Wednesday. She also put in place a protective order that limits who can see the unredacted records. A Fulton County spokesperson declined to comment on a pending legal matter. The State Election Board did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The FBI served a search warrant at the Fulton County elections hub on Jan. 28 seeking records related to the 2020 election, leaving with hundreds of boxes containing ballots and other records. The county unsuccessfully sought to have a judge order the return of the records, but the federal government did provide the county with what it said was a digital copy of the records that were taken. The overwhelmingly Democratic county, which includes most of the city of Atlanta, has been a target of President Donald Trump and his allies since he narrowly lost the presidential election in Georgia to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. Trump has consistently insisted without evidence that widespread voter fraud in the county cost him victory in the state. Multiple courts and state and federal officials have found no evidence of fraud that would have altered the outcome. A statement from an FBI agent supporting the search warrant used to take the records said the agency was examining possible “deficiencies or defects” in Fulton County’s 2020 vote count. More than six years after that election and 10 months after the records seizure, no charges have been filed. The FBI in July instructed field offices across the country to dedicate more than 200 staffers to its investigation of the 2020 election in Fulton County, describing it as a “priority investigation,” and The New York Times reported that the FBI and federal prosecutors last week interviewed the man who served as the county’s election director in 2020. A Trump-aligned majority on the State Election Board has repeatedly sought to reopen a case alleging wrongdoing by Fulton County during the 2020 election. The board in November 2024 served subpoenas on the county seeking records related to the 2020 election. County election officials asked a judge to quash the subpoenas. Fulton County Superior Court Judge Robert McBurney in December 2025 declined to quash the subpoenas, finding that the State Election Board’s inquiries “fell squarely within the SEB’s authority.” He ruled that the state board would have to bear the costs of producing the records it was seeking and a hearing on that matter was pending when the FBI seized the county’s records. As a result, McBurney put the case on hold. Ellerbe, who took over the case this year, held a hearing on the matter in October before issuing her order Tuesday. Her protective order says the State Election Board can use the records for its investigations but says the records cannot be disclosed to anyone other than people identified in the order, which includes the board members and staff, as well as experts they may consult.

articles.title: Mott Community College president fired
articles.description: The board terminated the employment agreement for President Shaunda Richardson-Snell, who served as Mott’s president for two years and faced controversies.
articles.content: Mott Community College trustees terminated without cause the presidency of Shaunda Richardson-Snell, who served as Mott’s leader for two years During her tenure, she faced several controversies including allegations that she asked a guest whether he had accepted Jesus Christ as his personal savior; an attorney later said she had been cleared of wrongdoing in those allegations Mott trustees appointed an interim president Mott Community College has fired President Shaunda Richardson-Snell without a reason, but her termination follows numerous controversies during her two-year tenure, including alleged “religious proselytizing” while serving in her official role. The college board’s attorney said she’d been cleared of wrongdoing in those allegations. Richardson-Snell could not be reached. Trustees of the Flint-based college voted Monday to end Richardson-Snell’s contract without cause and put her on administrative leave with her salary and benefits, according to a statement from the college. Richardson-Snell had about two years left on her contract. Board Chair Jeff Swanson, who did not attend the meeting because of medical reasons, said he didn’t know how long her paid administrative leave would last. He thought it would likely end when her contract expired. Swanson said he didn’t know why his fellow board members ended Richardson-Snell’s contract. RELATED: Mott College trustees to meet about complaint that president is ‘proselytizing’ Mott College trustees postpone action on alleged ‘proselytizing’ by president New allegation against Mott college president emerges The board also voted to appoint Marcus Matthews, Mott’s associate vice president and chief of staff, to serve as acting president, effective immediately. Four of the seven-member board were present and voted. None of those who voted could be reached for comment. Some are glad the chapter is behind the college.Donate “There’s been two years of controversy. It has preoccupied the college,” said Paul Jordan, a retired social worker who taught at Mott for more than a decade and attended Monday’s board meeting. “The college can move on now.” Richardson-Snell earned about $250,000 annually, sources said. Swanson said the board will meet soon to decide how to find the college’s next leader. “The board made a decision, I disagree with it but I will stand behind it,” Swanson said. “We have to come together as one board for the students.” Richardson-Snell began serving as Mott’s interim president in 2024 following the departure of Beverly Walker-Griffea, who became the first director of the Michigan Department of Lifelong Education, Advancement, and Potential. Richardson-Snell joined the college after “25 years of global, multi-industry leadership and financial management experience in both the non-profit and for-profit sectors” and has worked for General Motors, TI Fluid Systems, Trinity Health and Delphi Corporation, according to the college’s website. Some were concerned about the lack of education in her background. In 2025, she became the college’s permanent president without a national search. Richardson-Snell allegedly spoke with a student and a college guest about her Christian faith. In December, Americans United for Separation of Church and State sent letters to her and board members, asking it to stop. The board called a meeting to discuss the issue, prompting scores of community members to speak publicly in support of and against Richardson-Snell.

articles.title: Detroit moves closer to $2.2B redevelopment of iconic Renaissance Center
articles.description: The vote came just ahead of the council’s winter recess, and followed weeks of impassioned public debate from both sides and a flurry of information requests from council members over the mechanics and benefits tied to the complex set of agreements.
articles.content: Detroit City Council gave its go-ahead for the contentious $2.2 billion proposed makeover of the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront. After delaying a week in order to seek answers from General Motors Co. and Bedrock, council members voted 7-2 to approve about $473 million of vital tax incentives and an unprecedented $133.3 in community benefits. In addition to the public subsidies approved Tuesday, Detroit’s Downtown Development Authority has pledged $75 million in cash contributions, bringing the total public subsidies to over half a billion dollars. City Council President James Tate and Pro Tem Coleman A. Young II as well as members Scott Benson, Angela Whitfield-Calloway, Mary Waters, Renata Miller and Latisha Johnson voted for the measures. Council Members Gabriela Santiago-Romero and Denzel McCampbell voted no. The vote came just ahead of the council’s winter recess, and followed weeks of impassioned public debate from both sides and a flurry of information requests from council members over the mechanics and benefits tied to the complex set of agreements. The majority of council members in support cited the promise of jobs and next-level riverfront enhancements for the city’s young people, while those opposed said they didn’t feel the deal offered Detroiters enough and that it progressed too quickly. Related: RenCen seeks rebirth, visitors seek directions: A day inside Detroit landmark Should taxpayers pay bill for RenCen rehab? 2 Detroit RenCen towers could be torn down as part of new plan District 4 Council Member Latisha Johnson said she only decided Tuesday morning to vote for the redevelopment based on a resolution crafted with Mayor Mary Sheffield’s support that would direct the $90 million the development will pay instead of taxes (payments-in-lieu-of-taxes, or PILOT) for affordable housing, neighborhood beautification and anti-poverty efforts beyond downtown and midtown. While she had been conflicted, Johnson said she couldn’t “deprive Detroiters from being able to access jobs.” District 2 Council Member Angela Whitfield-Calloway. (City of Detroit photo) Members Angela Whitfield-Calloway, Renata Miller and Mary Waters also spoke at length about why they are for the redevelopment plans. Whitfield-Calloway shared some of her personal history with the RenCen, including that it was the site of her high school prom, and noted that she’d been proactive in seeking answers about the development since it was announced in 2024. Donate Detroiters, she said, had “never really enjoyed it (the riverfront)” in her lifetime like visitors can in other major American cities. Supporting the project, she added, would give young people something to do on the riverfront where there is currently “nothing” to do but walk from one end to the other and back. She encouraged the developers to expedite the project — but not “cut corners” — so she and others could see it in their lifetime. “It’s time for newness. It’s time for evolution, right? It’s time for opportunity. It’s time for opening up our horizons,” she said. The plan calls for the $1.6 billion redevelopment of the RenCen towers, including the “deconstruction” of two of the five, and using the remaining for housing, office space and other amenities. The remaining $624 million will go toward an entertainment-centered buildout of several acres of nearby land along the East Riverfront. Waters said that she too wanted Detroit to be a “destination place” with a, “Navy Pier like Chicago,” which she said would answer the calls of young Detroiters. “I hope that we can all evolve to get to this place where we welcome people from all over the country, all over the world, to our city because we have such a fantastic riverfront,” Waters said. Detroit City Council Member Mary Waters. Credit: City of Detroit Waters also addressed persistent complaints about the community benefits process and the recommendations put forth by the Neighborhood Advisory Council seated to negotiate on behalf of impacted neighbors of the RenCen project, saying “maybe we should not have the NAC.” She also told the audience that she’s committed to making sure developers stay accountable to their commitments. “And, as long as God gives me the strength, I will monitor this project every step of the way. Detroiters, know that you can count on me to do exactly that,” Waters said Miller dismissed oft-repeated “rhetoric” about the fast pace of the community benefits process, and championed the job commitments. “This is the chance to build the best, most welcoming, family-friendly riverfront anywhere by Detroiters and for Detroiters,” Miller said. Council members Gabriela Santiago-Romero and Denzel Anton McCampbell — whose motion to postpone the vote until the new year failed — delivered the sole ‘no’ votes on all items except the PILOT resolution brought forward by Johnson. District 7 City Council Member Denzel McCampbell. Credit: City of Detroit McCampbell said that he and his staff found more than 120 instances of language in the community benefits agreement that “lacked enforcement mechanisms,” and still wanted more benefits for residents. Santiago-Romero maintained that the council should have taken more time and called on the developers to commit to a “human-centered design.” “If we did that, more people would be in support of this,” she said. “… I believe 90% of Detroiters want this. I believe 100% of them don’t want to feel as if they’re paying for it without their inputs.” Critics of the RenCen redevelopment have questioned the need for public subsidies given the project is a private development. The questions have only sharpened since Dan Gilbert’s recent nearly $1 billion pledge to establish a 501(c)4 nonprofit to own and manage the redevelopment. Bedrock’s CEO Jared Fleisher spoke before the council and to reporters on Tuesday, saying “everything is right” about the project and “everything was right about Dan’s heart and intent.” Fleisher also apologized for calling McCampbell’s questions about the necessity of public funding “indecent,” during a recent subcommittee meeting. GM and Bedrock sent a joint statement following the vote, saying they were grateful to the council and Sheffield’s administration, residents and the NAC for the work that led to the largest community benefits package in Detroit’s history. Tuesday’s vote also aligns with the developers self-imposed timeline to seek state tax breaks from the Michigan Strategic Fund before Gov.-Elect Jocelyn Benson takes office in January. ‘Job wages and benefits’ Nearly every seat in the council meeting room at the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center was filled Tuesday. A majority of the nearly 200 public commenters shared their thoughts on the RenCen in the allotted half a minute of speaking time online and in-person. People supporting and pushing back against the project repeated many of the same sentiments that have circulated for weeks. The project’s supporters — who have consistently been represented in meetings by development, business, construction and labor interests — continued to discuss the proposed benefits to Detroiters at Tuesday’s meeting. Among the sea of pro-development attendees representing labor unions in different sets of matching high viz gear — including construction, demolition and auto unions — one benefit was king: jobs. John Ford was one of the many Labors Local 1191 members who donned orange and touted the jobs the development would bring, pre- and post-construction. “It’s about job wages and benefits. It’s about the future of Detroit and for my family,” Ford said. “Without it (the development), it’s like death to my family.” Much of the remaining pro-development support came from residents, religious leaders, business owners, community and business developers, and more pleading on behalf of benefits like entertainment and tourist opportunities. Many also spoke about the benefit to the youth and Detroit’s future. “I come from a time where the majority of downtown was abandoned, so I would dreadfully fear to see GM or the GM building become abandoned as well,” said District 5 resident Darnell Wanni. Detroit City Council Member Renata Miller (left) Gabriela Santiago-Romero (center) and Latisha Johnson (right). Credit: City of Detroit However, the amount and security of the negotiated benefits are what the project’s many critics — as well as several of the council members — have been sharply questioning. Residents, advocates and Santiago-Romero have said the size and complicated nature of the project and its financing more than warranted more time. U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Detroit, and State Rep.-elect Chris Gilmer-Hill spoke at Tuesday’s council meeting and during a morning demonstration hosted by Detroit Action and the Detroit People’s Platform. Tlaib joined others in championing accountability concerns and what they deemed as a lack of transparency involved in the development’s agreements and proceedings. This includes a still-confidential Law Department memo related to revenue sharing and community ownership feasibility, as well as and the non-disclosure agreement between the Detroit Economic Growth Corp. and developers that has restricted public access to the project’s financial information. Tlaib referenced the No Secret Deals Act, recent legislation she penned that would prohibit the use of such NDAs. Only a small contingent of community members continue to ask for redevelopment to be stopped or for all five RenCen towers to be “saved.” Those speaking out against the development and developers primarily called on council to delay action until the new year in order for questions to be answered and more favorable benefits. “Nobody here is against development,” said Detroit Action’s Alejandro Navarrete during Tuesday’s meeting, but added that opponents do take issue with “rushing the democratic process” and with “CEO bullies trying to tell us what questions we can and cannot ask” in exchange for subsidies. “If you don’t delay and don’t do your due diligence in negotiating with the developer, then this is what we’re leaving on the table,” Navarrete said.

articles.title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
articles.description: Perseverance is having trouble transmitting to Earth. Odyssey is rapidly burning through its waning fuel supply.
articles.content: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks. The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history. Losing its voice The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
articles.description: Internal memos reveal a “Code Red” overhaul and ambitious one-hour recovery goals.
articles.content: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide. Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote. The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Citing legal concerns, Whitmer orders EGLE to halt Line 5 tunnel permit activity
articles.description: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced Tuesday she was putting environmental permit considerations for the Enbridge’s Line 5 tunnel project on ice, until the state can resolve legal questions raised by the state Supreme Court over the summer. The 645-mile pipeline running from northwest Wisconsin to southwest Ontario includes a 4.5 mile dual segment resting on […]
articles.content: "Shut Down Line 5 - No Tunnel" sign on the grounds of the Michigan Capitol. | Laina G. StebbinsMichigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer announced Tuesday she was putting environmental permit considerations for the Enbridge’s Line 5 tunnel project on ice, until the state can resolve legal questions raised by the state Supreme Court over the summer. The 645-mile pipeline running from northwest Wisconsin to southwest Ontario includes a 4.5 mile dual segment resting on the bed of the Straits of Mackinac, where Lake Michigan and Lake Huron meet. At the end of July, the Michigan Supreme Court ordered the Michigan Public Service Commission to revisit its decision to issue a permit for the controversial project. The court ruled that the commission, which regulates Michigan’s energy and utility companies, had not properly considered the environmental harms that could arise from extending the lifespan of the oil pipeline. In September, the governor directed the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to examine how the Supreme Court ruling affects its permitting decisions. This map shows the proposed tunnel and the existing dual pipelines crossing the Straits of Mackinac. | Screenshot from the MPSC Line 5 Issue Brief Following Whitmer’s announcement, pipeline opponents filed two separate requests for a contested case on a set of permits EGLE approved in July, arguing that the tunnel project posed a serious threat to the environment and the lifeways and cultural resources of Native American tribes in the region. EGLE has yet to issue a decision on a National Pollution Discharge Elimination System permit, which would allow Enbridge to release up to 6 million gallons of wastewater created during construction into the Great Lakes, after treating it at one of two sites on opposing ends of the Straits of Mackinac. “Protecting the Great Lakes and the people who depend on them has been a top priority of mine since day one,” Whitmer said in a statement on Tuesday. “I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water. Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life. Given what is at stake, and the Michigan Supreme Court’s recent decision, I have directed EGLE to suspend further action on its Line 5 Tunnel Project permits at this time. Michigan will continue to put the protection of our water, environment, public health, and communities first.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE EGLE Strategic Communications Advisor Scott Dean confirmed the department was suspending further permitting action until the legal questions are resolved. “Taking a step back until we have greater clarity is the right thing to do for the Great Lakes, our natural resources, and the communities whose livelihoods depend on them,” the department said in a statement. Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy said the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision to revoke the permit from the public service commission had introduced new uncertainty as the company aims to secure the permits needed to move forward with the tunnel, “even as the permitting record remains strong.” “The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy issued permits in July 2026 and previously in 2021. Both permitting rounds included detailed technical reviews, public meetings, hearings, and consideration of thousands of public comments,” Duffy said in a statement. “They also involved extensive interaction between Michigan’s tribal leaders and state agencies.” Photo by Laina G. Stebbins The fight against Line 5 has stretched on for years, with tribal nations and environmental advocates calling for the pipeline to be shut down. “This decision is not the finish line,” Whitney Gravelle, president of the Bay Mills Indian Community said. “Our responsibility to protect the Great Lakes does not end with a pause in permitting. Tribal Nations have been here since time immemorial, and we will be here long after any corporation has come and gone. We must keep fighting for our waters, demand that our voices are heard, and ensure that decisions affecting our homelands respect our rights and responsibilities. The future of the Great Lakes must be shaped by those who have care for these waters, not by the interests of corporations seeking to profit from them. We have a responsibility to future generations, and we will not stop speaking up or standing up for the Great Lakes.” In response to concerns that the pipeline may rupture, spilling crude oil into the Great Lakes, Enbridge agreed to replace the dual pipelines with a new segment, housed within a utility tunnel buried beneath the lakebed. In her 2018 campaign for governor, Whitmer promised to take action against the pipeline, later revoking and terminating Enbridge’s easement to operate the pipeline within the Great Lakes. Enbridge has since taken legal action against Whitmer and the director of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, arguing that federal regulations and a 1977 treaty between the United States and Canada bar the state from terminating the easement. While Judge Robert Jonker of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan deemed Whitmer’s move to revoke the easement unenforceable, the governor and DNR Director Scott Bowen appealed the case to U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit. Arguments in the case are scheduled for Dec. 15.
