articles.title: Trump pardons West Virginia turkeys, Freedom and Feathers
articles.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump pardoned two turkeys named Freedom and Feathers Tuesday, a Thanksgiving White House tradition that dates back to the George H.W. Bush administration. Trump used the brief event on the White House South Lawn to tout renovations, including a new granite helipad and progress on the ballroom, where he said next […]
articles.content: President Donald Trump grants a presidential pardon to Freedom, the National Thanksgiving turkey, as, left to right, National Turkey Federation Chairwoman Christy Puffenbarger, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., look on during the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation on the South Lawn of the White House on Nov. 24, 2026 in Washington, D.C. The turkeys, Freedom and Feathers, were raised and trained at Deans Gap Farm in Fort Seybert, West Virginia, by Scott and Becky Rightsell. Freedom and Feathers will retire to Texas A&M University following the ceremonial pardon. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump pardoned two turkeys named Freedom and Feathers Tuesday, a Thanksgiving White House tradition that dates back to the George H.W. Bush administration. Trump used the brief event on the White House South Lawn to tout renovations, including a new granite helipad and progress on the ballroom, where he said next year’s turkeys will receive accommodations. The two turkeys this year from West Virginia, presented by the trade group the National Turkey Federation, stayed in a suite at the nearby luxury Willard InterContinental Hotel. “Unfortunately for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests. They’ve done this for a long time. We’ve saved a lot of turkeys, but I’m pleased to announce that next year we’ll be able to have a special location right over there,” Trump said, signaling to the construction site for a 90,000-square-foot ballroom where the East Wing stood. Construction has continued after the U.S. Supreme Court stayed an injunction in August against further progress on the structure. The modern White House turkey pardon began in 1989, according to the White House Historical Association. The tradition of presenting a turkey to the president began with President Harry Truman, the association says. Trump acknowledged West Virginia farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell, who raised the turkeys on their farm in Pendleton County. “We won West Virginia by 45 points. At least I did when I was on the ballot,” Trump said, inflating his margin in the 2024 presidential election. He defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in the state by 41.9 percentage points, according to The Associated Press. “I don’t know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me,” Trump said. Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have attributed the drubbing to the administration’s ongoing war with Iran, which significantly raised gas and diesel prices. Outgoing U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., stood beside Trump as he delivered the traditional pardon. Johnson has announced he will not remain in House Republican leadership after Democrats overwhelmingly won the majority of the House in the 2026 midterms. All national Republican incumbents in West Virginia won their races. Trump hosted the pardon just hours after he awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani. The medal is considered the nation’s highest civilian honor. Giuliani was instrumental in perpetuating Trump’s false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election.

articles.title: Walmart teams up with Meta to bring Black Friday deals to AI agent Muse
articles.description: Walmart now lets customers shop Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.
articles.content: Shopping with AI is becoming less of a futuristic idea and more of something companies expect us to do. Walmart is the latest retailer making that shift, teaming up with Meta to let customers shop its Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent. The partnership, announced Tuesday, gives shoppers another way to find products, compare prices, and make purchases without browsing Walmart’s website themselves. Instead, customers can simply tell Muse what they are looking for and let the AI do the work. The announcement highlights how differently Walmart and Amazon are approaching AI shopping. While Amazon has taken steps to stop third-party AI agents from making purchases for customers, Walmart is leaning into the idea. To get started, users open the Muse app, sign in to their Walmart account, and return to the assistant to begin shopping. They can ask it to find specific products, compare options, or track down deals. Once a customer makes a request in Muse, the assistant sends it to Walmart, which returns relevant products and helps build a shopping cart. Walmart says it has built privacy protections into the experience. For instance, Muse doesn’t get access to a customer’s Walmart shopping history or other personal information. Shoppers can also set spending limits, require approval before purchases, and review orders placed by the agent. Plus, the company notes users can always delete their agent’s profile if they want to. The experience is powered by Walmart’s Agent Gateway, a new system that allows outside AI assistants to connect directly with the retailer’s online store. This launched in October, and the company is planning to open it up to more developers and AI platforms, meaning Muse could eventually be just one of several assistants capable of shopping Walmart’s online store. Walmart is not the only company teaming up with Meta’s Muse. Instacart also recently joined forces with the AI assistant. Beyond Muse, Walmart has recently rolled out more AI-powered features to its own shopping assistant, Sparky. Some of the newer additions include turning handwritten shopping lists into shopping carts, using photos and voice commands to find products, and helping customers get around their local store. Shoppers can search for an item and use a pin on the store map to see exactly which aisle it’s in. There’s also a “Flash Price Tag” button that makes the item’s shelf label light up. Turkey production bounces back but prices still rise
articles.description: Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports. Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected status for many […]
articles.content: Turkeys gather for feeding at Whiffletree Farm in Virginia in September. Turkey production is up this year after two years of decline but prices rose because of strong demand and a shortage of whole birds. (Photo courtesy of Whiffletree Farm)Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports. Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected status for many immigrants take a toll on their workforce. Many producers support proposed bipartisan federal legislation to give them more access to visas for temporary workers. Disruptions to Temporary Protected Status for some immigrants “could create significant operational challenges and further tighten an already constrained labor market,” Leslee Oden, CEO of the National Turkey Federation, wrote in an October op-ed supporting the federal visa legislation. Top state turkey production, 2025 Minnesota – 33.5 million birds North Carolina – 28.0 million birds Arkansas – 21.5 million birds Indiana – 20.0 million birds Virginia – 15.3 million birds Missouri – 14.7 million birds Iowa – 10.8 million birds Pennsylvania – 7.6 million birds “This is a good first step to help packers and processors keep the rural economy moving and to ensure American consumers have access to affordable food,” Meat Institute CEO Julie Anna Potts said in a statement earlier this year. Minnesota, North Carolina and Arkansas last year had the highest turkey production numbers, and millions of turkeys were also produced in Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Virginia, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture report. Wholesale prices shot up to a projected $1.76 a pound for whole hen turkeys this year from $1.36 last year and just 94 cents in 2024, according to the USDA, a 30% one-year increase. But a Farm Bureau report found retail prices for turkey up only about 10% from last year as retailers used turkey promotions to draw customers – some reported prices as low as 69 cents per pound. Production increased this year to 5.1 billion pounds, after dropping two years in a row to as low as 4.8 billion pounds last year, but it’s still well below 2020’s 5.7 billion, according to the USDA report. “They’ve had a lot of disease pressure over the years, so they’re still building up production numbers. That being said, grocery stores love to offer turkey deals,” said Farm Bureau Deputy Chief Economist Faith Parum in a November podcast. Jesse Straight, who sells about 1,000 turkeys a year directly to customers at his Whiffletree Farm in Warrenton, Virginia, said he hasn’t been as affected by labor and disease issues as other, larger operations. His birds live outside on pastures with more fresh air than factory farms, and he pays a small staff fair wages, he said. “We get people coming to our farm from all over the country because they believe in our mission,” Straight said. “Our mission is to heal the land and give the animals a life that fits their nature, and heal our customers through good food.” Nationwide, higher prices in most areas do not translate into more money for farmers, Farm Bureau Associate Economist Cameron Castillo told Stateline. “Significantly higher costs are prohibiting farmers from capturing any economic benefit this year,” he said. Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org. articles.title: Llegó a Michigan en busca de seguridad. Tras ser deportada, fue asesinada en Venezuela.
articles.description: Huyendo de la violencia por ser trans, Q llegó a Michigan en busca de una vida mejor. Pero tras ser agredida sexualmente dentro de un centro de detención, fue deportada a Venezuela. Meses después, fue asesinada.
articles.content: Q came to Michigan in 2025 seeking refuge after facing violence for being trans. In 2026, she was deported to Venezuela. (Jodi Westrick / Michigan Public )Read this story in English here.En el verano de 2025, Q buscaba comenzar una nueva vida cuando llegó a Pontiac, Michigan. Su sobrina, Rosaura Quintero, recuerda haberse sentido tranquila ante la posibilidad de esa nueva vida de Q en Estados Unidos."En parte, en confianza," dijo a Michigan Public. "Segura de que iba a estar mucho mejor. De que iba a tener de pronto el cuidado y la seguirdad de andar tranquila en una calle, trabajar tranquila y que nada ib a poder sucederle — cosa que aca en Venezuela no podia hacer." "En que iba a tener quizás el cuidado y la seguridad para caminar tranquila por una calle, trabajar tranquila, y que no le pudiera pasar nada, algo que aquí en Venezuela no podía hacer".En Venezuela, Q fue brutalmente golpeada por ser transgénero. Tenía cicatrices en el pecho que, según contó, le dejó un violento ataque con arma blanca."Acá tenía que mantener escondida, entre aparentar", dijo Quintero. "Temía por su vida".A principios de este año, Q le dijo a Michigan Public que creía haber sido atacada por su trabajo con su organización, Fundación LGBTI Gente Bella. La misión de la organización era defender los derechos de las personas LGBTQ+ y, al mismo tiempo, recaudar fondos para quienes los necesitaban.Q at an event hosted by her organization, Fundación LGBTI Gente Bella, where she joined fellow hairstylists in volunteering their time and skills to provide haircuts for older adults.(Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero)"Si fallecía alguien, eh, le colaboraban para un funeral, colaboraban para un entierro, para alguna cremación", recordo Quintero. "También organizaban operativos para ir a atender a personas digamos iban a ancianatos, les cortaban el cabello, los arreglaban, iban a hospitales, se donaba comidas, medicinas....todo lo que alguien pudiera necesitar que estuivera en sus posiblidades lo hacian".Nueva iglesia, amigos y barberia En Pontiac, Q comenzó a trabajar en una barbería local.Le contó a Michigan Public sobre el día en que tuvo la oportunidad de demostrar su talento para cortar el cabello al arreglar la peluca de una clienta que otro barbero había arruinado."Agarré esa peluca y le hice un corte fabuloso, estilo Whitney Houston, algo divino. La dejé espectacular", dijo.Su incipiente carrera como estilista en Estados Unidos se vio truncada cuando fue arrestada por el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) en febrero de 2026. En lugar de celebrar su cumpleaños número 50 con la familia que había elegido, Q terminó en una unidad para hombres del Centro de Procesamiento North Lake, en Baldwin, Michigan.En North Lake, Q fue agredida sexualmente durante varias semanas. Michigan Public no identifica a las víctimas de agresión sexual. Cuando denunció la agresión a la policía, fue examinada en un hospital, trasladada fuera del centro y rápidamente deportada a Venezuela.Volviendo a empezar en VenezuelaQ llegó a Caracas, Venezuela, en abril de este año y se instaló en su ciudad natal, Barquisimeto, con su hermana y su sobrina, Rosaura Quintero."La verdad, trataba de no relacionarse mucho, de no exponerse — mejor dicho a sufrir algún daño a la cual ya había sufrido mucho", dijo Quintero. Q loved her three dogs, Flecha (left), Vaca (middle) and Buda (right). She often referred to them as her children. (Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero )Ya de vuelta en casa, contó Quintero, Q pasaba mucho tiempo reencontrándose con sus tres perros, Flecha, Vaca y Buda, a quienes solía llamar sus hijos."Las recogía de la calle y las criaba.", dijo Quintero.Compartir la comida era una de las formas en que Q demostraba su amor, según Quintero. Los días en que a la familia no le alcanzaba el dinero para comprar comida, Q dejaba de comer para que sus perritos tuvieran algo que comer."Le encantaba cocinar para nosotras para dar, pero muchas veces ni comia, era como que por gusto lo hacia by bueno muy divino", agregó. Según Quintero, la comida favorita de Q eran las caraotas, como se les dice en Venezuela a los frijoles negros.'Fue quien nos sacó adelante'Durante 20 años, Q fue peluquera, un oficio, que en realidad comenzó cuando tenía unos 14 años."No había hecho cursos ni nada, sino que practicaba con mi abuela y mi mamá", dijo Quintero. Q worked as a hairstylist for several decades and was known for her balayage. (Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero )Con el paso del tiempo, sin embargo, Q logró convertirse en una de las mejores estilistas de la ciudad, según Quintero. Era conocida por su balayage, una técnica de mechas a mano alzada."Siempre que contaba su historia era muy cómico porque al principio pues como no sabía no le pagaban bien". dijo Quintero. " Llegó a hacer algunos daños en algunos cabellos mientras empezaba hasta que pasaron los años y se hizo grande — una de las mejores estilistas de de la ciudad". Fue cortando el cabello como Q logró mantener a su familia únicamente con sus ingresos, contó Quintero."Fue quien nos sacó adelante", dijo Quintero. "Mi mamá aprendió el oficio de la peluquería por ella. Hoy en día mi mamá también es una peluquera, gracias a ella que siempre la apoyó". Una firme defensora de las personas trans en Venezuela Defender a la comunidad LGBTQ era una de las grandes pasiones de Q."Era una férrea defensora de las personas queer, de las personas LGBTQ, especialmente de las personas trans en Venezuela", dijo Cisily Quintanilla Zuniga.Después de que Q fuera deportada, Zuniga se puso en contacto con ella a través del grupo defensor de los derechos de los inmigrantes No Detention Centers of Michigan."Yo era una amiga, una defensora y un enlace con Q para amplificar su historia aquí en Estados Unidos y ayudar con apoyo mientras ella está en Venezuela", dijo Zuniga.Q le dijo a Michigan Public que necesitaba someterse a una cirugía para tratar algunas de las lesiones que sufrió a raíz de la agresión sexual en North Lake. En octubre logró recibir esa atención. Q(Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero )"Hoy estoy sana y con muchas ganas de seguir trabajando por mi comunidad LGBTQ+. Agradezco el trabajo que todos hacen para apoyar a los demás. Dios observa todo. Dios lo ve todo", escribió Q en ese momento en un mensaje a Michigan Public.Aunque estar de vuelta en Venezuela no fue fácil para Q, Zuniga dijo que ella encontró mucho sentido en ayudar a quienes lo necesitaban."Cualquier comida que tuviera, la llevaba al hospital y trataba de alimentar a las personas en situación de calle".El sueño de Q, según Zuniga, era abrir un espacio físico para su organización, Fundación LGBTI Gente Bella, donde las personas LGBTQ pudieran construir comunidad y recibir apoyo y cuidados."Creo que su sueño era simplemente ser una mujer trans, someterse a una cirugía de afirmación de género", dijo Zuniga. "Tenía un caso sólido de asilo, tenía un caso sólido para buscar refugio en nuestro país e intentar vivir una vida en paz".El 2 de noviembre de 2026, Q fue atacada y golpeada casi hasta la muerte mientras intentaba hacer una de sus entregas habituales de comida a personas necesitadas, según su sobrina.Quintero dijo que solía acompañar a su tía en estos recorridos, pero que ese día no pudo. Recuerda que Q le dijo que no le importaba ir sola, que solo quería ayudar."Pero si no iba a hacer ese donativo, esa comida se iba a perder, habiendo tantas personas con hambre, jamás se lo iba a permitir". Según documentos del hospital que la familia de Q entregó a Michigan Public, Q recibió múltiples golpes en la cabeza y el cuerpo que le provocaron un traumatismo craneoencefálico severo.Once días después del ataque, la familia de Q tomó la difícil decisión de retirarle la asistencia respiratoria. Q murió el 13 de noviembre en la unidad de cuidados intensivos del Hospital Central Universitario "Dr. Antonio María Pineda", en Barquisimeto, Venezuela donde nacio. Tenía 50 años. Q(Courtesy / Q)"Perdí la persona más importante de mi vida. La única persona con la que contaba para todo", dijo Quintero. "Pero me sentiré siempre orgullosa de quien fue, de quien ere...y donde quiera que este, siempre le voy a agradecer todo lo que hizo con amer y todo lo que dio con amor para mi". Sus familiares y amigos, tanto en Venezuela como en Michigan, recuerdan a Q por su optimismo, su espíritu incansable y su determinación de hacer del mundo un lugar mejor.“Mira, en otra vida la volvería a escoger sin pensarlo como mi tía, como mi madre, como mi amiga incondicional", dijo Quintero. "Jamas la cambiaria". Cisily Quintanilla Zuniga dijo que No Detention Centers of Michigan está recaudando fondos para ayudar a la familia de Q a cubrir los gastos funerarios.

articles.title: Newborn vaccination rates for hepatitis B drop sharply
articles.description: The percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has declined sharply in recent years, falling to 65.6% in June 2026 from 79.8% in 2022, according to a new study published Nov. 24 in the New England Journal of Medicine. The authors of the peer-reviewed study looked at health records from more than 1.3 million […]
articles.content: A worker applies an adhesive bandage to a child at a vaccination clinic in Minneapolis’ Corcoran Park in August 2023. A new study found the nationwide percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccination has declined sharply since 2023. (Photo courtesy of the City of Minneapolis)The percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has declined sharply in recent years, falling to 65.6% in June 2026 from 79.8% in 2022, according to a new study published Nov. 24 in the New England Journal of Medicine. The authors of the peer-reviewed study looked at health records from more than 1.3 million infants and found that the percentage of babies receiving the hepatitis B vaccination within one day of birth began declining around 2023. The study also found that fewer mothers testing positive for hepatitis B got the vaccine for their babies, from around 98% of those infants in 2025 to around 94% in 2026. A panel of federal vaccine advisers, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, voted in December 2025 to end the longtime recommendation for infants to receive the hepatitis B vaccination at birth even if the mom tested negative. That decision is on hold pending legal challenges. The study was based on data from Truveta, a health data and analytics company owned and governed by 30 health systems across the nation. In explaining the December change, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said screening of pregnant women is highly reliable and can spot disease early. But Nina Masters, an author of the new study and a principal applied research scientist at Truveta specializing in infectious disease and maternal health, told Stateline that “not every mother is tested during pregnancy, and not every person who gets tested has a known status.” “And screening is imperfect,” she said. “This birth dose has been a universal recommendation to be a safety net to catch those kids that might fall through the cracks, and what we’re seeing here is that that safety net is kind of falling apart.” Hepatitis B is a contagious liver infection that can cause symptoms of fatigue, loss of appetite and jaundice, and potentially lead to cancer. But it can be prevented through a vaccination. The virus can be passed down from an infected mother to a baby, so since 1991, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recommended that all newborns receive the hepatitis B vaccination within a day after birth to prevent early infections, especially when mothers test positive. A 2023 study by CDC researchers found that between 1990 and 2019, with the recommendation for newborn vaccination, there was a 99% decline in reported cases of acute hepatitis B among people younger than 19 years old. But amid growing vaccination skepticism, the new study found that fewer babies are getting the shot. The shift began a few years before vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. became secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in February 2025. Researchers noted the decline in vaccination rates for hepatitis B comes as the federal government and many conservative states walk back vaccine mandates for children. Just this month, the United States lost its status as a country that had eliminated measles, as the transmission of measles has risen in the last year. Children are particularly susceptible to the disease. “When messaging gets confusing and there’s different recommendations coming from different medical bodies and different kinds of assessments of vaccine safety that are being publicized, I think it can become scary and hard to make the right choice,” Masters said. “And I think that’s what we’re seeing is just extreme confusion as a result of the level of misinformation and changing recommendations around pediatric vaccines.” Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org. A new Pew Research Center study found the population of Muslims will surpass that of Christians in the world by 2035. Conrad Hackett is the senior demographer and associate director of research at Pew Research Center. The research examines seven major religions around the world. “So for hundreds of years, Christians have been the largest group in the world, and Christian numbers are continuing to grow, but Muslims are growing at a faster rate than Christians…within a decade, there will be more Muslims around the world than there are Christians,” he says. Hackett states that change in religious populations is a result of demographics, birth and death rates globally, especially in sub-Saharan Africa where both religious groups will grow exponentially. He highlights the religious population increase that will happen in Africa, where women have more babies for both Christians and Muslims. “A lot of young people being in the population, that’s going to give momentum. Furthermore, life expectancy is increasing in Africa…more of the children born today and in recent decades are living longer than their parents and their grandparents lived,” he says. Although both populations will increase, Muslim populations are growing faster. “Globally, Muslim women had 3.1 children per woman, and Christian women had about 2.5 children per woman. Jews had 2.3 children per woman, and then remaining groups had a number of children per woman that’s below what demographers call the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman,” he says. The number of children a generation needs to replace itself over the long term, Hackett says. Many people do not identify with a religion, even though they occasionally follow some practices. China is home to the most people who do not identify with a religion. Hackett concludes that Jews and Hindus are increasing in number but decreasing as a share of the world’s population, while Buddhists and people of no religion are decreasing both in number and in population.

Two Women Sue East Lansing After Sidewalk Falls, One Into an Uncovered Manhole
articles.description: Both women sustained serious injuries, according to lawsuits filed in Ingham County Circuit Court.
articles.content: Two women are suing the city of East Lansing over injuries they sustained in separate falls involving unsecured utility openings in sidewalks, according to lawsuits filed in Ingham County Circuit Court. The first woman sustained serious leg injuries when she stepped into a utility hole that was not properly secured in April of 2025. Months later, a second woman fell into an uncovered manhole on the Harrison Road Bridge, where she was left trapped without a ladder and with a brain injury and fractured ribs, according to lawsuits filed in the Circuit Court. The city did not respond to a request for comment. Claire Gangware was walking with her husband in East Lansing on the sidewalk along Grand River Avenue near Raising Cane’s on April 26, 2025. Her husband stepped on an unsecured, bent utility cover on the sidewalk just before her, moving the cover enough that it acted as a “trap door,” Gangware’s lawsuit says. The fall caused several injuries to her left leg, including a fracture to her foot that has required two surgeries. Due to the injuries to her left leg, Gangware began overcompensating with her right leg, which aggravated degeneration in her right knee, according to her lawsuit. “She’s going to have problems now for the rest of her life as a result of her injuries,” Theodore Larkin, attorney for Gangware, told East Lansing Info in an interview. A section of Michigan state law dealing with a municipality’s duty to “maintain the sidewalk in reasonable repair” states that a municipality can’t be held liable for breaching that duty unless it can be proven that the municipality knew, or should have known for at least 30 days prior to the injury, that a defect in the sidewalk existed. The defect also must also create a vertical discontinuity defect of at least 2 inches in the sidewalk or create a dangerous condition in the sidewalk other than a vertical discontinuity. Larkin said the warped utility cover created both hazards. According to court records, the city argues that Gangware can’t establish that the city had knowledge of the askew utility cover. Further, the city argues the utility cover in question is owned and maintained by the Lansing Board of Water and Light and is their responsibility. “The sidewalk where plaintiff allegedly fell was maintained in reasonable repair by the City of East Lansing such that it was reasonably safe and convenient for public travel,” a filing submitted by the city’s attorneys in September reads. On Oct. 29, Ingham County Circuit Court Judge Rosemarie Aquilina denied East Lansing’s motion of Non-Party At Fault where the city argued they were not the responsible party for any of the injuries Gangware’s lawsuit outlines. “…the City of East Lansing had an exclusive duty to repair the alleged “dangerous condition in the sidewalk” and/or “vertical disconformity defect of 2 inches or more in the sidewalk” if it is proven such a condition and/or defect existed,” Aquilina’s decision reads, adding that the Lansing Board of Water and Light does not bear such duty. Just a few months after Gangware was hurt, in the early morning of Sept. 12, 2025, a Michigan State University student fell into an uncovered steam vault in East Lansing, where she was trapped with a host of injuries, according to another lawsuit filed in Ingham County Circuit Court in November of this year. The MSU student was walking on the sidewalk along the Harrison Road Bridge on MSU’s campus when she fell into an uncovered steam vault manhole. She remained trapped without a ladder in the steam vault. The manhole “lacked various safety devices allowing an unknown third-party to remove it,” the MSU student’s lawsuit reads. The fall resulted in scarring and disfigurement, a brain injury, fractured ribs and injuries to the woman’s teeth and pelvis. The MSU student experiences persistent pain and disability due to the fall, the lawsuit says. In July of 2025, MSU initiated repair work on the steam vault that was involved in the student’s injury. Construction entities that were contracted to do engineering and design work, Clark Dietz and Fishbeck Thompson, did not include a locking mechanism for the manhole cover, which was also designed to be too small to properly fit the steam vault hole, the lawsuit asserts. It was foreseeable that someone could remove the steam vault lid in this high foot traffic area of campus, the lawsuit says. The student’s attorney, Michael Laurila told ELi in an interview there is a presumption that the cover was removed by an unknown third party, but the legal argument is that the defendants had a responsibility to secure the cover. Though other defendants in the case Granger Construction Company and Ram Construction Services had installed other steam vault lids on MSU campus, the lawsuit asserts that despite their knowledge and experience, the defendants placed the defective lid. “When installing the lids, Defendants Granger and/or Ram knew that the lids lacked any sort of locking mechanism and were too small for the manhole yet completed the work as if it was safe,” the lawsuit reads. “Despite this actual and/or constructive knowledge, at no point did Defendants Granger or Ram question either the university, Clark Dietz or Fishbeck regarding this reckless design.” After the installation of the defective and unlocked manhole cover, the lawsuit asserts Granger Construction Company and Ram Construction Services continued work at the Harrison Road Bridge and had “ample opportunity” to perceive the danger the lid posed and rectify it. The City of East Lansing bears some responsibility, according to the lawsuit. The city reviewed plans to repair the steam vault prior to construction beginning and should have noticed that a locking mechanism for the lid was not included, posing a safety issue on the sidewalk it is responsible for maintaining, the student’s attorney argues. “While it is believed that MSU controls the sidewalks on campus (i.e. where this sidewalk on the Harrison Road bridge is), by nature of its role as the State, MSU cannot be statutorily required to repair and/or maintain a sidewalk,” the lawsuit reads. articles.content: The Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (RSTMH) and the World Health Organization (WHO) are convening a webinar to showcase the mid-term evaluation of the NTD road map 2021–2030, published on 4 November as the Global report on neglected tropical diseases 2026. Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affect more than 1 billion people, predominantly those living in poverty, or remote or fragile settings, and with limited access to essential health services. Ending the neglect to attain the Sustainable Development Goals: a road map for neglected tropical diseases 2021–2030 (“the road map”), endorsed by the Seventy-third World Health Assembly in 2020, set targets for the prevention, control, elimination and eradication of 20 diseases and disease groups, since expanded to 21 with the addition of noma in December 2023. The year 2025 marked the midpoint of implementation of the road map, making it a timely moment to evaluate progress and recalibrate priorities for the second half of the decade. This mid-term evaluation examines implementation and impact during 2021–2025 and provides recommendations for 2026–2030. The mid-term evaluation combines a quantitative analysis of 71 global indicators with a structured qualitative assessment across 11 dimensions, informed by more than 350 experts, programme managers, policy-makers and partners. This 90-minute webinar will open with WHO leadership and an overview of the mid-term evaluation’s findings. Speakers will then discuss the key priorities identified in the report, the lessons learned from 2021–2025 and the way forward to 2030. There will be time for audience questions. articles.title: UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
articles.description: The British cyber agency says that "building strong foundations has never mattered more" as AI hacking tools rely on exploiting simple security flaws.
articles.content: The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks. The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post. The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed. The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds. While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices. “Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote. The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data. The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.” The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes. articles.title: Northern Michigan clean energy jobs up in 2025, defying statewide trend
articles.description: This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Northern Michigan saw an uptick in people working in clean energy last year. That’s contrary to the rest of the state, as changes to federal policies scaled back jobs in a sector that’s a key part […]
articles.content: In this file photo, volunteers from Leelanau Energy assist with the installation of solar panels at the Northport-Leelanau Wastewater Treatment Plant in 2012 (Photo courtesy of Joe DeFors)This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Northern Michigan saw an uptick in people working in clean energy last year. That’s contrary to the rest of the state, as changes to federal policies scaled back jobs in a sector that’s a key part of addressing climate change. The numbers come from the annual Clean Jobs Midwest report, released last week by the clean energy advocacy group E2. The report uses yearly federal survey data collected by the U.S. Department of Energy. Northern Michigan added 278 clean energy jobs last year, an increase of nearly 10 percent over 2024. Wexford County saw the most growth, followed by Kalkaska and Grand Traverse counties. “When people think about clean energy jobs, they often picture large manufacturing facilities around Detroit, or other major population centers. But one of the things that our data shows is that that’s only part of the story,” said Micaela Preskill, director of state advocacy at E2. The majority of clean energy growth in the country is happening in rural areas, according to research. Renewable energy developers are often drawn by access to natural resources like large tracts of land or water, and northern Michigan is no exception. In Wexford County, 250 jobs were added last year in “microgrids,” small-scale electric grids that can generate, store and provide power to a localized area, even in the event of a broader grid outage. There are signs that the county’s industry will likely continue to grow, as the City of Cadillac seeks to convert its municipal buildings into a microgrid powered with renewable energy, using $4.4 million from the energy efficiency company Budderfly. Michigan has ambitious clean energy goals. In counties along the Lake Michigan coastline, the state has already invested millions of dollars to boost the region’s “Blue Economy” through electric boats, which don’t use fossil fuels, and powering ports with clean energy. And a new state siting law curbs local governments’ ability to flat-out reject big solar, wind and battery projects. Still, large-scale clean energy growth in the region faces backlash from some local residents, many who say the projects take away productive farmland. Despite some jobs gains, seven other counties in northern Michigan saw decreases in clean energy jobs, mirroring the rest of the state. Preskill said the drop is a direct result of the federal policy changes that have stalled investment and reversed short-term progress. Michigan lost about 2,000 jobs in clean energy in 2025, or a 1.5% decrease from the year prior. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025 reversed many of the clean energy policies put in place by the Biden administration — policies that led to gains in clean energy jobs across Michigan and the country. Rebate programs for electric vehicles, heat pumps and other home energy upgrades went away. According to the report, Michigan was hit hardest by cuts to electric vehicle programs. The transportation sector saw the largest cuts, making up the majority of losses in the state. But even with fewer clean energy jobs, the report maintains that there’s a lot of long-term growth. Since 2020, clean energy jobs in Michigan have grown by more than 12 percent. And jobs in solar and wind made up the largest portion of power generation jobs in Michigan last year, continuing to surpass jobs in fossil fuels like natural gas and coal. Preskill with E2 said future growth in the state hinges on federal policy. Climate activists around the country saw this month’s historic “blue wave” midterm elections as a win, as Democrats secured congressional majorities that could reverse many of the Republican cuts under the current administration. “We had a recipe that was working,” Preskill said. “Growing policy uncertainty and project cancellations could slow that momentum, just as many rural communities are beginning to see the benefits.”

3 Michigan training programs pass first step for new federal grant
articles.description: Michigan has approved three short-term training programs to seek final approval from the federal government for participation in the new Workforce Pell, a historic expansion of the Pell Grant for more students.
articles.content: Three short-term training programs have gotten state approval for Workforce Pell, the expansion of the federal Pell Grant for students seeking credentials in programs lasting eight to 14 weeks Federal officials issue final approval The US Department of Education has approved three dozen programs in eight states for Workforce Pell since it launched earlier this summer While 42 programs offering short-term professional training sought Michigan’s approval, three made the cut for potentially becoming eligible for the new federal Workforce Pell Grant. State officials declined to name the programs because they still need final approval by the US Department of Education. The 39 programs that applied but didn’t get the state’s approval did not yet meet the 70% job placement or completion required by federal regulations, said Erica Quealy, spokesperson for the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity. Workforce Pell is an expansion of the Pell Grant — federal funds that have been awarded for more than 50 years to low-income students seeking a certificate, associate or bachelor’s degree. Launched in July, Workforce Pell is the first time students can apply for the federal grant if they are seeking a short-term credential that takes eight to 14 weeks to complete. Proponents say getting into a high-skill, high-wage, in-demand job sometimes takes weeks, not years. Costs will now be more affordable with Workforce Pell, they say, for those choosing shorter training programs in various fields such as healthcare, information technology, skilled trades and early childhood education. RELATED: Michigan targets prosperity in plan to boost training and wages for workers Michigan’s new, free community college program: What you need to know EMU offers women a chance to earn bachelor’s degrees in prison Experts say programs approved so far for Workforce Pell can cost upward of $5,000. Until now, students paid out of pocket. Though Michigan approved three programs for potentially getting final approval for Workforce Pell, state officials are continuing to work with many of the programs that didn’t get sanctioned to help them resubmit applications, Quealy said. “The State of Michigan is committed to a long-term partnership with training providers to scale the program so Michiganders across the state can access this aid to train for in-demand careers,” Quealy said. Workforce Pell was part of the Trump administration’s 2025 Working Families Tax Cuts Act, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.Donate Since it officially launched last summer, the federal government has approved about three dozen programs in eight states, including last week’s approval of a program for medical assistants in New York. Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent called it “an important milestone in expanding affordable, career-focused education opportunities … (so) students can gain the skills employers need and enter high-demand fields more quickly, while helping address critical workforce shortages in industries like healthcare.” It’s not surprising that it is taking time to set up Workforce Pell, since states have to vet programs seeking to participate to ensure they meet federal eligibility requirements, said Chris Madaio, senior advisor at The Institute for College Access and Success. Those requirements include that the program must be at an accredited school and have a 70% completion rate and job placement rate “This program can have really good success for students if the state does a really good job of enforcing those requirements and rules and even considers adding their own rules to ensure that these programs are affordable and lead to meaningful credentials,” Madaio said. Additionally, the federal government expected the process to unfold slowly and it’s good that it is, Madaio said. “We don’t want to open the floodgates and anybody, including the bad actors or the low-quality programs, get in,” Madaio said. “It is important that students have access to affordable programs that lead to meaningful credentials and improve their employment and earning prospects.” Lindsey Reichlin Cruse, director of research at National Skills Coalition, added that vetting programs for Workforce Pell is creating important outcomes following a history of education not being in sync with workforce needs. “It has offered states a sense of urgency to do some of this alignment across workforce and education systems that we’ve all been talking about,” said Reichlin Cruse. Nine community colleges and one proprietary school submitted 42 programs for Michigan to consider in the first round of applications, Quealy said. Michigan will reopen its Workforce Pell approval application in January and will offer support to training providers to submit successful program applications with a webinar series, model application and individual meetings. “As workforce needs change,” Quealy said, “local Workforce Boards, postsecondary institutions, employers, and community-based organizations can utilize (Workforce) Pell to adapt or build high-quality programs aligned to regional labor market needs, and we are eager to support such efforts.”

articles.title: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real
articles.description: Technical details are still limited, but we already know it's fun to drive.
articles.content: Porsche provided flights from Albany, New York, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the 718 EV prototype. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. It wasn't until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche's upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle. That's not particularly low for a sports car, but it's practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that's usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed. So, for the company's first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Democrats plan investigations of Trump. Here’s how his Justice Department is fighting back.
articles.description: As the Trump administration prepares for Democrats to launch an onslaught of investigations in the next Congress, the U.S. Department of Justice is turning to a three-word phrase to preemptively fight back: “Legitimate legislative purpose.” The Justice Department has sent letters in recent days to leading Democratic lawmakers raising the possibility they’ll face criminal prosecution […]
articles.content: A banner showing President Donald Trump hangs on the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 20, 2026. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)As the Trump administration prepares for Democrats to launch an onslaught of investigations in the next Congress, the U.S. Department of Justice is turning to a three-word phrase to preemptively fight back: “Legitimate legislative purpose.” The Justice Department has sent letters in recent days to leading Democratic lawmakers raising the possibility they’ll face criminal prosecution for conducting aggressive oversight of President Donald Trump and his aides. Legal experts have widely dismissed the threats as empty because the U.S. Constitution affords lawmakers wide protections from prosecution for official actions taken in Congress. But the letters — and that short phrase within them — offer a blueprint for how the White House will try to undermine the investigations themselves, in addition to discrediting the investigators. Democrats will take control of Congress with majorities in both the House and Senate in early January. Line of attack The Justice Department is signaling it will attack congressional subpoenas seeking documents and testimony from federal officials as driven by retribution and outside the bounds of traditional oversight. The government appears ready to argue such requests cross a line into illegality. The DOJ letters allege Democrats intend to violate federal laws that prohibit individuals acting in an official capacity from violating the constitutional rights of others. In this case, those supposedly having their rights violated would be Trump’s associates. “As you should know, whatever investigations you and your fellow Democrats have planned must have a legitimate legislative purpose,” U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, the top Justice Department official in the Southern District of Texas, wrote on Nov. 19 to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat. Reitz, a former Republican candidate for Texas attorney general, included similar language in letters to Rep. Robert Garcia and Sen. Adam Schiff of California, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. All are Democrats likely to play prominent roles in investigating the Trump administration after the party takes control of Congress in January. Additionally, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, in a Nov. 9 letter to Garcia wrote that “abusive and capricious threats” were spreading among Democratic legislators. He warned that the Trump administration “will not be extorted” and expected lawmakers to investigate within settled constitutional limits. Rocky 2 years ahead The defiant posture comes as Trump braces for a final two years in office marked by aggressive oversight from House and Senate committees, as Democrats probe alleged corruption and mismanagement. Many Democrats credit the blue tsunami that gave the party large majorities in both chambers to voters’ frustration with self-enrichment by Trump and other government officials. In addition to the Justice Department letters, Trump on Nov. 20 signed an executive order that requires federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information. Contractors are also required to abide by any White House instructions to withhold communications that the Trump administration says are covered by executive privilege. Democrats are now on a collision course with the Trump administration that could end up in the courts. Raskin pressed forward with his oversight efforts despite Reitz’s letters. The ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Raskin sent letters on Nov. 20 to the DOJ, FBI, Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the U.S. Bureau of Prisons — demanding that they preserve all records, including Signal chats, which can be set to auto-delete. Slotkin responded to Reitz in a letter last week, calling congressional oversight an important constitutional responsibility. She called the DOJ official’s threats frivolous and a violation of his ethical duties as an attorney. The nonpartisan watchdog group Campaign for Accountability has filed a complaint against Reitz with the State Bar of Texas. “I’m not going to participate in some sham investigation,” Slotkin said in a video response to Reitz. “Every American has freedom of speech. In particular, senators have special privileges and special responsibilities given by the Constitution for oversight.” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told States Newsroom that Trump is willing to work with anyone “to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans.” “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” Bis said in a statement. The Justice Department didn’t respond to a request for comment. The U.S. Supreme Court has previously ruled Congress has broad power to investigate the federal government. Broad oversight authority Constitutional law experts interviewed by States Newsroom said that while lawmakers don’t have unlimited investigative power, their oversight authority is sweeping, rooted in the need for lawmakers to have information before legislating. “Although they are not stated in the Constitution, there is a clear line of cases that say as long as investigations are related to possible legislation, then they can proceed,” said John Vile, a professor of political science at Middle Tennessee State University who has written books on constitutional law. In 1957, the Supreme Court found that the U.S. House Un-American Activities Committee had exceeded the bounds of congressional power after labor organizer John Watkins was prosecuted for refusing to answer lawmakers’ questions about whether certain individuals were members of the Communist Party. The court threw out Watkins’ conviction, finding his due process rights were violated. Retiz cites the case, known as Watkins vs. United States, in his letters to Democrats as he warns lawmakers that their planned investigations could be unlawful. In the court’s 6-1 decision, Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that investigations solely to punish or for the “personal aggrandizement” of the investigators weren’t permissible. Unmentioned by Reitz is that earlier in the same paragraph, Warren wrote that Congress’s power to investigate is “broad” and encompasses looking into both how current law is being applied and possible future law. “It includes surveys of defects in our social, economic or political system for the purpose of enabling the Congress to remedy them,” Warren wrote. “It comprehends probes into departments of the Federal Government to expose corruption, inefficiency or waste.” As recently as 2020, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the sweeping scope of Congress’ investigatory powers. In a 7-2 decision in a case called Trump vs. Mazars USA, the justices didn’t immediately allow a congressional subpoena for Trump’s personal financial records to proceed, but they repeated Watkins’ description of lawmakers’ sweeping oversight authority. “The congressional power to obtain information is ‘broad’ and ‘indispensable,’” Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in the majority opinion. The speech or debate clause Whatever the courts may decide about future subpoenas, constitutional scholars in recent weeks have been virtually unanimous in arguing that the Constitution’s speech or debate clause will protect Democratic lawmakers from criminal cases for launching congressional investigations into the Trump administration. The clause says of lawmakers that “for any Speech or Debate in either House, they shall not be questioned in any other Place.” The provision has its roots in England, where members of Parliament used to fear prosecution for offending the crown. Its protections have been on display as recently as October, when federal agents searched the D.C. residence of Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Democrat. Recently unsealed court documents show a federal judge asked prosecutors for additional information on the “potential Speech or Debate Clause implications” of the search before signing off on a warrant. Steve Vladeck, a professor of federal courts at Georgetown University Law Center and a leading expert on the Supreme Court, wrote on Nov. 23 that an indictment alleging lawmakers had conspired to deprive individuals of their rights through a “weaponized” oversight process would mean proving the illegitimacy of the investigation’s subpoenas, hearings or committee votes. “Every one of those is a legislative act, for which the members’ motives are off the table,” Vladeck wrote in his newsletter, One First. “When the oversight itself is the alleged crime, the Speech or Debate Clause is arguably at its zenith.” Lawmakers also can’t be sued for their speech in Congress, a protection that they sometimes use to make remarks that might otherwise open them up to allegations of defamation. Last year, Rep. Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican, accused her ex-fiance and three other men of being sexual “predators” in an explosive speech on the House floor. A federal judge later dismissed a defamation lawsuit brought against Mace by one of the men. Illegal orders video The Trump administration has also so far failed in other efforts to target Democratic lawmakers over their communications. Just over a year ago, several lawmakers with military or national security backgrounds, including Slotkin, posted a video telling members of the military and intelligence community that they should refuse illegal orders. Trump called the video evidence of seditious behavior and as recently as this month asked whether the lawmakers would ever face prosecution. The Department of Defense attempted to demote one of the lawmakers, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired U.S. Navy captain. A federal judge has temporarily blocked the demotion, but the Trump administration has appealed the decision. But even without prosecutions, Molly Nixon, a senior fellow in executive power at the libertarian Cato Institute, said the White House can still work to slow down investigations. The letters and the recent executive order serve as “markers” that could deter cooperation with Congress, she indicated. Individuals pressed for information might weigh the pros and cons of quick and full compliance. “The fact that if I were a member of Congress I would not be particularly worried about a successful criminal prosecution doesn’t mean the administration doesn’t have a lot of tools at its disposal,” Nixon said.

articles.title: Golden Girls bills could bring together older and younger roommates
articles.description: Twenty-five-year-old Californian Regnar Madarang wants to own his own home someday. But the Bay Area’s rent of $2,000 and up for a single room wouldn’t allow him to save up for a downpayment, he said. Three months ago, Madarang learned from a friend about the California-based homesharing platform JoeyCo, which connects homeowners with students and […]
articles.content: Twenty-five-year-old Regnar Madarang rents and lives with Eileen and Gary Ruppel, who are in their 70s, in Palo Alto, California, through a homesharing agreement. Some states are passing laws to allow more unrelated people to share a home. (Photo courtesy of Regnar Madarang)Twenty-five-year-old Californian Regnar Madarang wants to own his own home someday. But the Bay Area’s rent of $2,000 and up for a single room wouldn’t allow him to save up for a downpayment, he said. Three months ago, Madarang learned from a friend about the California-based homesharing platform JoeyCo, which connects homeowners with students and young people who rent a room and do spare work around the house. He now lives with Eileen and Gary Ruppel, who are in their 70s, in Palo Alto. He particularly likes visiting local museums with the couple and says they have allowed him to find community. “I’ve learned so much from them and it’s a living situation where I get to help around the house and build community with people who know so much about the neighborhood … and it doesn’t hurt the budget,” Madarang said. “Homesharing is a give and take. They opened their home to me so I also want to add whatever I can to their life.” Beyond private apps, some cities, including San Francisco, Boston and New York City, have homesharing programs that promote intergenerational living. So do some states such as Pennsylvania and Vermont. But many other areas have laws limiting the number of non-related people who can live in a home. To address that barrier, lawmakers in several states have introduced or enacted so-called Golden Girls legislation, named after the hit TV show about four older women who share a home. The measures create a statewide standard that allows unrelated individuals to live in the same home. Local jurisdictions still could set occupancy limits based on health and safety standards. Supporters say these bills can boost the housing supply and open up a living arrangement that can help tackle the high cost of housing and combat senior loneliness. But opponents say that statewide mandates override local authority on housing and zoning issues and could allow single-family housing to be turned into crowded boarding homes. Several groups are advocating for similar versions of Golden Girls model legislation they want states to pass, including the American Legislative Exchange Council or ALEC, the Metropolitan Abundance Project and the Pacific Legal Foundation. In Pennsylvania, a Golden Girls bill sponsored by Democratic Rep. Tarik Khan passed the House 123–78 in June, but stalled in the state Senate. Some fellow Democrats voted against it, saying they wanted to protect local zoning authority. Khan said his first post-college home was a two-bedroom apartment that he shared with three other guys and cost them $2,000 in monthly rent while he worked retail jobs. Khan believes uncapping the amount of unrelated people who can live with each other is one of the ways to lower the cost of housing without additional funding or construction. “We could increase the availability of housing by doing this,” he said to Stateline. “We can lower the cost of housing without breaking the bank.” Pennsylvania Republican state Rep. Jeremy Shaffer had concerns about a Golden Girls bill overriding local authority and undercutting occupancy limits intended to enforce health and safety standards. “Basically, this bill would allow any single-family home to essentially become a de facto small apartment building,” said Shaffer, as reported by the Pennsylvania Capital-Star. A report by the conservative Pacific Legal Foundation found that nine of the 10 largest Pennsylvania cities limited the amount of unrelated roommates to three or four people. Thirty-two states have enacted no laws protecting unrelated roommate living arrangements, and municipalities in all those states have restricted how many unrelated people can share a home, according to a July 2026 analysis by the foundation, which advocates removing those limits. “Most states are silent on this topic,” said Kyle Sweetland, a research manager for property rights at the foundation, which takes cases on limited government, property rights and individual rights. Since 2017, Colorado, Iowa, New Hampshire, Oregon, Texas and Washington have passed laws prohibiting some local governments from limiting the amount of non-related residents that can occupy a single home. In Connecticut, a Golden Girls measure that would have required towns to allow homeowners to rent rooms to long-term tenants passed the state Senate with bipartisan support this year. But Democratic House Speaker Matt Ritter declined to bring it up for a vote in the House, according to the CT Mirror. Ritter worried about how a provision requiring homes to be owner-occupied would be enforced and feared people would buy housing as rental property and lower homeownership rates in cities like Hartford, the outlet reported. JoeyCo’s founder Alison Donnally believes homesharing is an underutilized housing option that could help bridge generational lines among younger and older adults affected by a multifaceted housing crisis. “You walk the dog, you pick up the groceries, you act as a good roommate, basically, you get paid to be a good roommate, right?” said Donnally. “You’re not just sort of drifting and floating in this housing market and you’re able to connect and put down roots in a way that is hard to find in other housing options that are available right now.” City limits In Maryland, Annapolis Alderman Brooks Schandelmeier, a Democrat, said the city’s newly-passed ordinance “Bedrooms for People Act” allows homeowners to rent spare bedrooms without risking $1,000-a-day fines. Schandelmeier once rented a bedroom in a home to afford to live in the city, and said his legislation was inspired by an older constituent of his who needed income by renting a room in her home. “This is already happening throughout the city but it was just happening off the books,” he told Stateline. “People may ask, ‘Who would want to live with strangers?’ but I was once that person and it suited my life at the time. Others should also have a chance option if they want it.” He recalled a former councilmember boasting that previous enforcement of the law prompted the removal of five people from a home when a neighbor complained. “I’m hearing this story here and all I’m thinking about is that five people were thrown out onto the street and she’s bragging about it,” he said. “I don’t think the city should be interested in enforcing an outdated law that removes people from a shelter that was offered to them.” PadSplit, which says it’s the largest co-living room rental platform, is in favor of Golden Girls measures and any policy that lifts roommate or home sharing caps. Its founder Atticus LeBlanc thinks Golden Girls legislation is good low-hanging fruit for housing policy on the state level and should be a bipartisan solution for accommodating changing housing habits and affordability. “Pretty much everybody should be able to support that one,” LeBlanc said about Golden Girls legislation. “That’s a series of actions on the state level where it shouldn’t matter where you fall on the political spectrum.” LeBlanc told Stateline that he recently emailed the Arlington City Council in Texas about neighbors’ opposition to more than four unrelated people sharing a house. “I think there’s a misconception that it’s this sociability piece driving this housing behavior when it’s almost entirely financial,” LeBlanc said. “Your housing option shouldn’t be restricted based on how many relatives you have.” Arlington City Council held sessions this year during which some city officials said they are leery of these types of housing options. Arlington’s definition of family is a single housekeeping unit with “no more than four individuals unrelated to the head of household by blood, marriage or adoption.” In August, the city’s Code Compliance Services Director Alex Busken said investors and companies were purchasing single-family homes and renting them to multiple tenants, sometimes with more than five occupants. Some owners had obtained permits to add bedrooms. Housing pressures across generations According to the Urban Institute, the share of young adults ages 25 to 34 who are homeowners fell from 40% in 2005 to 29% in 2024. Jung Hyun Choi, a principal research associate in the Housing Finance Policy Center at the Urban Institute, said higher borrowing costs and lower savings have reversed some of the progress young adults made toward independent living and homeownership between 2019 and 2022. One part of that equation is the relationship between home prices and interest rates. “So we’re in this market where it’s like both are very, very high, so it’s very challenging for younger adults to find a home that they can purchase,” she told Stateline. Older adults face their own headwinds in today’s housing market. In 2023, more than a third of households led by someone 65 or older spent over 30% of their income on housing. About half of these households, or 6.7 million, spent over 50%, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. The center’s 2026 State of the Nation’s Housing report found that households headed by someone 65+ are now dissolving at a rate of 1.4 million per year due to deaths, move-ins with family or entry into care facilities. Those households also have the highest housing cost-burden rate of any age group. Younger adults are trying to afford their first homes, while older adults face rising costs that threaten their ability to remain in familiar homes and communities, said Jenn Jones, vice president for financial security and livable communities in AARP’s office of government affairs. “Who knew that sort of housing affordability would be bringing generations together, right?” she said. Madison Daniels, a senior external relations adviser for AARP, told Stateline the organization advocates for laws that support home sharing, which can generate supplemental income for older homeowners and be more affordable than living alone. Back in Palo Alto, Madrang has three months left until his contract with the Ruppels is up. Both sides seem keen to re-up. Homeownership is still in the sights for Madarang but for now, he’s found a home and a family that is worth delaying that milestone for. “I dream of one day owning property and not having to rent anymore. But the reality is that it might not be possible at this moment,” Madarang said. “For where I am now, homesharing works for me. It’s home.” Stateline reporter Robbie Sequeira can be reached at rsequeira@stateline.org. This story was originally produced by Stateline, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Michigan Advance, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

articles.content: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.” Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes. [Media: https://www.threads.com/@peterbaker/post/DgHHIz1FRpO] It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.” In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email. It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information. Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
articles.description: You can learn a surprising amount from a few loose teeth.
articles.content: Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world. The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans. A handful of teeth with a lot to say Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.Read full article Comments

articles.title: WHO Director-General announces support for vaccines, medical equipment during official visit to Cuba
articles.content: Today, World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced US$2 million to help strengthen Cuba’s national immunization activities and provided essential medical equipment to health facilities. Dr Tedros arrived in Cuba on 22 November at the invitation of Cuba’s Minister of Public Health, Dr José Ángel Portal Miranda. During his visit, Dr Tedros toured health facilities and met with President Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez. He was joined by senior officials from WHO and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). WHO’s new funding will support Cuban health sector priorities, with a focus on the National Immunization Program, especially vaccination for children and adults. Cuba has maintained very high vaccination coverage, of above 98%, for many years. In 2025, coverage decreased to 95%. WHO’s contribution will support immunization for approximately 62 000 newborns, more than 780 000 girls and boys, and over 110 000 people in other risk groups, as well as support rabies prevention and control actions. “Cuba’s hard-won public health achievements must be protected,” said Dr Tedros. “WHO/PAHO’s provision of essential vaccines is the latest demonstration of our commitment to support Cuba through significant health challenges and help maintain access to essential health services. Together with our partners, we will continue to stand with the Cuban people to protect health, save lives and sustain progress.” During his visit, Dr Tedros reaffirmed WHO/PAHO’s continuing support for the country's health services, and ways to protect progress in public health. Strengthening health cooperation was a central topic of Dr Tedros’s visit to Cuba. Between 2025 and 2026, WHO and PAHO have mobilized more than US$14 million through 14 projects to support the quality and sustainability of health services and strengthen health workforce capacities. During his mission, Dr Tedros visited the "William Soler" University Pediatric Hospital and the pediatric cardiocenter of the same name, meeting health workers and families of children receiving care there. The delegation delivered supplies and medical equipment mobilized with the support of the PAHO/WHO Emergency team, including basic medical care kits and equipment to strengthen the institution's response capacity: electronic monitors for blood pressure measurement; ophthalmoscopes/otoscopes, pulse oximeters, sphygmomanometers, stethoscopes, thermometers, among other resources. Dr Tedros also held discussions with the United Nations Country Team and other cooperation partners in Cuba on sustaining financial and strategic support for the country’s public health sector. These meetings identified new opportunities to expand collaboration and coordination according to the country's main health needs. The WHO Director-General was also updated by executives from Cuba’s main biotechnology companies on advances and challenges to the country’s pharmaceutical industry, which are developing new products in the areas of infectious disease prevention and control, Alzheimer's, cancer, and diabetes. This was Dr Tedros’s second official visit to Cuba as WHO Director-General. His previous visit took place in 2018.
