articles.title: What is SIP trunking? A business guide to modern calls
articles.description: Learn what is SIP trunking, how it works, what it costs, how to choose a provider, and how to connect it to AI voice agents for customer service.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) trunking is a technology that allows businesses to make and receive voice calls over the internet. SIP trunking helps businesses scale their customer service systems without the high costs and complex installation processes of physical phone lines. This is particularly helpful for businesses implementing AI voice agents, which aren’t inherently compatible with traditional phone systems. If you’re looking for a way to scale your business’s phone system efficiently, SIP trunking may be an effective solution. In this guide, we’ll explore how SIP trunking works, why it’s effective for growing businesses, how to choose a SIP trunking provider, and how to use SIP trunking with AI agents. SIP trunking is the process of connecting your business’s phone system to public phone networks using the internet, rather than using traditional copper phone lines. SIP trunking uses Session Initiation Protocol to connect your internal Private Branch Exchange (PBX) system to the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN). Then, you can send voice calls over this virtual connection. Some providers also support video calls and text messages. The SIP trunking process starts with signaling, which involves setting up the process and connecting the caller with the correct destination. The signaling process may also involve redirecting a call or closing a call once it’s over. Once the call has been set up, the data packets travel over a separate Real-time Transport Protocol, or RTP, not over the SIP itself. The data packets transmitted during a call are called ‘media’. Session Initiation Protocol, or SIP, is a signaling protocol that sets up, manages, and ends calls between two endpoints. In this case, the endpoints are your internal phone system and your SIP trunking provider, which connects you to the public phone network. A SIP trunk is the specific virtual connection that facilitates the call. One SIP trunk can contain multiple channels and handle dozens or even hundreds of calls at the same time. Voice over Internet Protocol, or VoIP, is a general term for any voice call that happens over the internet. SIP trunking is a specific VoIP method that connects your company’s internal PBX to the public phone network to facilitate calls. SIP trunking offers a number of benefits for growing businesses, especially when they need to expand their phone systems to support a higher volume of calls. Here are some of the advantages of using SIP trunking for your phone systems. SIP trunking is generally cheaper than using traditional phone lines, especially at scale. That’s because SIP trunks run over the internet connection you’re already using, so you don’t need to pay to install and maintain separate phone lines. With SIP trunking, you also typically avoid the high long-distance charges of traditional phone lines, because calls travel over the internet instead of separate circuits. International rates still apply and vary by provider, but they’re often lower than what physical lines charge, which makes SIP trunking a cost-effective option for organizations operating internationally. SIP trunking is primarily used for voice calls. Some providers also support video calls and business texting, and you can connect AI voice agents to your SIP trunk to handle customer service calls. This means you can use the same system to handle many different types of business communications. As your business grows, SIP trunking systems scale with you. You can add more channels to your SIP trunks quickly as your call volume grows. To scale a traditional phone system, you’ll need to bring in a technician to install new physical lines, which is both time-consuming and expensive. SIP trunking is much more flexible. You don’t have to change your business’s phone number when you switch from a physical phone connection to SIP trunking. This is particularly helpful if you already have a toll-free phone number that’s part of your brand identity. Many SIP trunking providers allow you to keep your existing carrier and phone numbers when you make the switch. You can also use local number porting to keep your phone number while switching to a new carrier. With SIP trunking, you can configure your phone calls to reroute to a backup system in the event of a power outage or other performance issue. This means you’re far less likely to miss an important call, and you’ll provide consistently reliable service for your customers. Calls happening on a SIP trunk can be encrypted for privacy and security. Some SIP trunking providers also offer access control features, which allow you to limit who uses your business phone system and who they can call. If a threat actor gets access to your phone systems, it could expose sensitive data or put your business at risk of a cyber attack. Using these security features helps reduce these risks. There are two primary factors that affect the cost of your SIP trunking system: the number of channels you have and the number of minutes you use each month. If you have an unlimited SIP trunking plan, you’ll be charged based on the number of channels you have. If you have a metered plan, you’ll be charged based on the number of minutes you use. Metered plans tend to be more cost-effective for small businesses that only need a few channels. However, unlimited plans are more cost-effective for large or fast-growing businesses with many channels operating continuously. Some SIP trunking providers also charge one-time fees for setup and number porting, or add-on fees for features like Direct Inward Dial (DID) numbers, toll-free numbers, business texting, call recording, or call rerouting. Providers may also charge higher fees for international calls, although they still tend to be much cheaper than long-distance calls on a physical phone line. There are many SIP trunking providers on the market, and you’ll need to determine which one best fits your business’s needs. Here are key factors to consider when choosing a SIP trunking provider: With voice AI, you can scale your customer service operations without hiring more agents. With ElevenAgents, you can route your inbound calls to AI agents using your SIP INVITE address. AI agents can also make calls through your SIP trunk with a configured hostname. ElevenAgents supports TLS encryption for call signaling, and you can enable SRTP media encryption. ElevenAgents supports access control with SIP trunking for businesses that need it. This happens using either a username and password (digest authentication) or Access Control List authentication. If your business requires IP allowlisting, ElevenLabs offers SIP servers with static IP addresses for Enterprise accounts. If you connect a SIP trunk to ElevenAgents, ElevenLabs doesn’t charge an extra fee for SIP trunking, and you pay your trunking provider separately for channels and minutes. ElevenAgents conversation minutes are billed on top of that, with LLM usage billed separately. Concurrency rises with your plan, up to 40 concurrent calls on Business, and Enterprise plans offer higher limits. With ElevenAgents, you can connect your existing SIP trunk so AI voice agents handle inbound and outbound customer calls in over 90 languages. ElevenAgents works with providers including Twilio, Telnyx, Vonage, Sinch, and Plivo, and supports TLS, SRTP, and digest or IP-based authentication. SIP trunking uses the internet to make phone calls. It uses Session Initiation Protocol to connect your business’s phone system to public phone networks. A traditional phone line uses copper wires and circuit networks to make voice calls. The number of channels you need depends on how many calls your team handles at the same time. High-volume call centers or sales teams may need even more channels. To calculate how many channels you’ll need, count the number of calls happening at the same time when your business is at peak capacity. You’ll need at least that many channels, plus a buffer for unexpected activity spikes. SIP trunking is not inherently secure, but you can add security features to protect your systems and data. Notably, you can encrypt both the signaling and media transfer processes for an added layer of protection. PRI is a legacy ISDN connection that delivers a fixed block of channels over physical copper lines, typically 23 channels on a T1 and 30 on an E1. SIP trunking carries calls over your internet connection, so you can add or remove channels in software instead of ordering new circuits. SIP trunking is typically cheaper and more flexible, while PRI uses dedicated bandwidth that doesn’t depend on your internet quality. SIP trunking connects a phone system you manage, such as your PBX, to the public phone network. A hosted PBX or UCaaS platform is a phone system that a vendor runs for you in the cloud, usually with features like voicemail, conferencing, and messaging, and it often uses SIP trunking behind the scenes. Choose SIP trunking if you want to keep control of your phone system or connect AI voice agents to it. Choose hosted PBX or UCaaS if you’d rather have a vendor manage the system. You need a SIP-compatible PBX or phone system, a SIP trunking provider, and enough bandwidth, roughly 80 to 100 Kbps per simultaneous call with the G.711 codec. Your system should support a common audio codec such as G.711 (PCMU or PCMA) or G.722. A session border controller (SBC) sits at the edge of your network to secure and manage SIP traffic, and your firewall must allow SIP signaling (typically port 5060, or 5061 for TLS) and the port range your provider uses for media. Ypsilanti Township officials vow to fight University of Michigan, Los Alamos project
articles.description: Public officials are pledging to continue fighting the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory’s planned Ypsilanti Township computing center after a vote green-lighting the facility’s construction. The university refers to the $1.25 billion project as a “high performance computing center,” and opponents say it’s a data center. The project is planned for 144 […]
articles.content: A rendering of a planned $1.25 billion Ypsilanti Township computing facility's lobby. Courtesy of the University of Michigan.Public officials are pledging to continue fighting the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory’s planned Ypsilanti Township computing center after a vote green-lighting the facility’s construction. The university refers to the $1.25 billion project as a “high performance computing center,” and opponents say it’s a data center. The project is planned for 144 acres adjacent to the Huron River on Textile Road in Ypsilanti Township. The university says it will use the facility for medical, energy, and computing research. The university’s Board of Regents voted Thursday to proceed with work on the project, approving construction costs of up to $785 million. Ypsilanti Township Attorney Doug Winters said the township will use every legal means necessary to stop the data center, including challenging the University of Michigan’s constitutional autonomy under state law. Michigan’s Constitution gives university boards general supervision of their institutions and control and direction of all expenditures from the institutions’ funds. The university did not respond to a question about a possible legal challenge. “U of M has gone far afield when it comes to the constitutional autonomy which they have enjoyed by virtue of being a university,” Winters said at a Thursday panel discussion at Eastern Michigan University, noting that most of the project’s capacity is for Los Alamos. The project does not serve an educational purpose for the university, he said. A university informational page on the project says Los Alamos will bring specialized computing technology and expertise that benefits the university’s educational mission and research. Los Alamos will use the facility for nuclear weapons research, The Michigan Daily reported in January, citing a Los Alamos deputy lab director. The lab developed the world’s first atomic weapons. Panelists say project will add to region’s environmental justice issues The University of Michigan will commit $5 million to community projects in the Ypsilanti area over the next five years, outgoing President Domenico Grasso said in a Thursday statement. The promise left speakers at the EMU discussion unmoved. “We don’t want your community benefits,” Winters told a crowd of hundreds, which responded with loud applause. A price cannot be put on environmental justice, clean air, and democracy, he said. Ypsilanti Township resident Lindsay Passmore holds a sign at a Nov. 19, 2026 EMU panel discussion on the Textile Road computing center project. Photo by Brian Allnutt/Planet Detroit. As a state university, Michigan does not require local zoning approval for the project to move forward. Community leaders previously said the university’s project will create costs for the neighboring community of Ypsilanti Township, which has more low-income areas and communities of color than Ann Arbor, without providing substantial benefits. Panelists said the project would compound environmental justice issues in Southeast Michigan, furthering nuclear weapons technologies, and potentially disturbing Native American cultural sites. Michigan says the project won’t impact the Huron River, which borders the property, and will create 30 to 50 technical support jobs; 200 higher-level research jobs; and 300 temporary construction jobs. United Tribes of Michigan backs Ypsilanti Township State Rep. Jimmie Wilson Jr., a Ypsilanti Democrat, said he’s optimistic Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson will follow through with a campaign promise to sign a moratorium on data center developments, he said Thursday. Lawmakers are motivated to send this legislation to her desk in January, Wilson said. Wilson, who won reelection Nov. 3, would support legislation backed by retiring state Rep. Reggie Miller, a Van Buren Township Democrat, including a bill to bar public officials from signing nondisclosure agreements when discussing data centers. The United Tribes of Michigan, a collaborative alliance of Michigan’s 12 federally recognized tribes, has weighed in on the issue. UTM passed a resolution that backs a consultation by the university with state tribes, and supports Ypsilanti Township’s efforts to modify the development. Ypsilanti Township is in an area that tribes used for river and trail travel, and includes burial sites and locations indicating Indigenous use, the resolution says. The Detroit Free Press reported that Scott Slagor, cultural resource protection manager at the State Historic Preservation Office, notified university project manager Rob Green that a site boundary with a recorded cemetery overlaps with the property. Green said on a Thursday press call that early property and historical record reviews have not identified any specific cultural site on the property. He acknowledged the work is not a substitute for ongoing professional review or tribal consultation. Jamie Stuck, Michigan tribal legislative liaison, told the crowd at EMU that tribes have a legal status that mandates such consultations. Ypsilanti Township Supervisor Brenda Stumbo, left, state Rep. Jimmie Wilson Jr. and township attorney Doug Winters at a Nov. 19, 2026 panel discussion at Eastern Michigan University. Photo by Brian Allnutt/Planet Detroit. Role of Los Alamos draws scrutiny Jay Coghlan, executive director of the organization Nuclear Watch New Mexico, said Thursday that the project is a bad deal for the state and the university, adding that it will benefit Los Alamos far more than the university. Los Alamos did not respond to a request for comment on this story. Patricia Hurn, an interim Michigan vice president for research and innovation, said on the university’s press call that its project is starting with a 50 MW capacity. Los Alamos is expected to use around 90% of the project’s power. According to the 2024 grant request, Los Alamos is slated to provide $300 million in funding for the project, while $850 million will be provided by the university and strategic value partner debt financing. The project received a $100 million grant in 2024 from the Michigan Strategic Fund and the Michigan Economic Development Corp., a taxpayer-funded agency providing business incentives. The project’s overall cost is $1.25 billion. In a Sept. 16 letter, U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) asked the university’s Grasso whether Los Alamos’ $300 million commitment of funds is contingent on site selection and regulatory and environmental approvals. Grasso replied Oct. 8 that “LANL has made no commitment of funds.” Steve Ceccio, the computing center project lead and a Michigan professor of mechanical engineering, said the first phase of the project will bring tenants to the facility, and Los Alamos is the principal tenant. “So upfront, Los Alamos or the tenants aren’t investing capital into the project, but they would help us defray the cost,” he told reporters Thursday. The rent will recover both the operational costs for the facility and the capital cost of its construction, Ceccio said. As part of the overall memorandum of understanding, the tenant would bring some of its own computational resources that would contribute to the overall total for the project, he said. articles.title: Commentary: Elissa Slotkin understands the Democratic mandate. Does the rest of her party?
articles.description: U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin gets it. Slotkin appears to understand that the “blue tsunami” that swept through the country on Nov. 3 is, in many ways, like an actual tsunami. Its initial force can be devastating, but eventually, the water recedes. What remains is what those who rode the wave to power intend to do […]
articles.content: WASHINGTON, DC - DECEMBER 11: Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) walks into the Senate Chamber on December 11, 2025 in Washington, DC. Two opposing health care bills intended to avert rising health care premiums have failed. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin gets it. Slotkin appears to understand that the “blue tsunami” that swept through the country on Nov. 3 is, in many ways, like an actual tsunami. Its initial force can be devastating, but eventually, the water recedes. What remains is what those who rode the wave to power intend to do with the opportunities it has created. Having built her political reputation by eking out victories in a politically competitive mid-Michigan congressional district, Slotkin was not necessarily someone many observers expected to emerge as a leading voice for systemic change in the hidebound U.S. Senate. She has often been characterized as a centrist whose political instincts were shaped by the need to win over voters who don’t necessarily even identify as Democrats. Yet she has increasingly been out front in demonstrating that pragmatism does not have to mean endless rounds of trying to build a consensus with those who view compromise as a dirty word. Facing new DOJ threats, Slotkin uses anniversary of illegal orders video to decry intimidation When Slotkin announced last week that she would support Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s challenge to longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, she did more than just add her name to a growing call for a new generation of party leadership. She took the extra step of challenging Democratic leaders to explain what they intend to accomplish during the first 100 days of the new Congress. As she put it, voters aren’t looking for “small nibbling at the edges.” They want bold policies that put more money in people’s pockets, and they want it fast. That is a significant and long overdue departure from the political playbook Democrats have followed for much of the past three decades. For too long, the Democratic Party has occupied a carefully calibrated political center, making incremental changes designed not to inspire those who voted them in, but instead to avoid scaring away voters who might otherwise lean Republican. This so-called Third Way politics popularized during Bill Clinton’s presidency got its name by Democrats triangulating against their political opponents but also what were viewed as the extreme members of their own party. But the wave that swept Democrats into power didn’t just wreak havoc on the Republican Party and the MAGA movement. It also swept away, whether its leaders care to admit it or not, the assumption that Democrats must continue to be guided by a political framework developed in the 1990s, before most of the 18 to 29-year-olds that powered the blue tsunami were even born. The threat matrix facing Democrats now isn’t that they will overreach by pursuing an ambitious legislative agenda. It is that they will fail to respond to the clear mandate for change that voters gave them. And this is where Slotkin’s background in the intelligence field is particularly useful. Intelligence analysis is, at its core, about assessing threats and recognizing patterns. By anticipating what comes next and distinguishing between the immediate crisis and the larger strategic picture, that analysis, if used properly, can be used as a map of where the pitfalls are and how to most effectively achieve the objective. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE And the objective for Democrats must be to demonstrate that democratic government can actually deliver meaningful improvements in people’s lives. So instead of looking back 30 years for inspiration, the party might best look back nearly a century to the first 100 days of Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency in 1933. FDR inherited a country in the depths of the Great Depression, with failing financial institutions and mass unemployment. But more importantly, the country had serious doubts about the future of democratic self-government. Whether we want to admit it or not, that is largely where we find ourselves today. But faced with that doubt, FDR didn’t cautiously advance modest reforms, but instead moved with unprecedented urgency, pushing through a series of sweeping legislative and executive actions that fundamentally reshaped the federal government’s relationship to its citizens. What we know now as The New Deal was not a single legislative achievement, nor was it perfectly executed. Many of its programs were challenged and later had to be revised or even curtailed. But the lesson of those first 100 days was that Roosevelt wasn’t interested in preserving the political status quo. He understood that the mandate from voters was to change it. Slotkin ‘seriously’ considering presidential bid, says decision could come soon That is the kind of ambition Democrats should be discussing now, not modest adjustments designed primarily to avoid offending the opposition. And while President Trump will hold the veto pen, making it unlikely much legislation will actually become law, Democrats need to make him use it. Ending the undeclared war with Iran, rolling back the incomprehensibly stupid tariff regime, raising the federal minimum wage and unwinding the termination of ACA tax credits should only be the beginning. Making a concrete case for Medicare for All and putting it to a vote has to be a priority. If the votes aren’t there to pass it, then let its opponents, including Sen. Slotkin, be on the record and explain why. But in each of these cases, the excuse that Trump will just veto it can’t be a reason not to try. Slotkin’s support for Van Hollen is significant not because the Senate leadership contest will determine the future of the Democratic Party, but because it reflects a larger debate about what the party intends to do with its newfound political power. Her insistence that prospective leaders present a concrete plan for their first 100 days is exactly the kind of demand for accountability that Democrats should be championing. The political waters will eventually recede. The question is whether Democrats will have built something durable on the ground they gained, or whether they will simply watch the tide go out and wonder where their opportunity went. Slotkin seems to understand the difference. The rest of her party would be wise to catch up.

A blast at a hot pot eatery in Vietnam’s capital Hanoi kills 6 and injures more than a dozen
articles.content: HANOI, Vietnam (AP) — An explosion at a hot pot eatery in Vietnam’s capital on Tuesday, suspected to have been caused by a gas leak, killed six people, injured more than a dozen others and damaged nearby houses. VnExpress, an online news outlet, said that the early morning blast in Hanoi shattered windows, cracked walls and tore metal shutters from their frames, while corrugated roofs and awnings collapsed. The report said that the explosion damaged nearby houses and shook neighboring apartment buildings, with debris scattered across the street. Police are using detection equipment to search for survivors and hydraulic machinery to lift concrete slabs, amid concerns that more people may be trapped under the rubble as the eatery was packed when the blast struck, the report said. Authorities have also relocated residents from neighboring buildings deemed structurally unsafe, it said. Hanoi police were cited as saying that investigations were ongoing. But preliminary findings pointed to a gas explosion that brought down part of the building. More than 14 people, including one with a traumatic brain injury, have been hospitalized, the report said. Lan Phuong, 26, told VnExpress that the blast jolted her and her younger sister awake, sending their balcony door flying about three meters (10 feet). “Luckily, we were both covered by blankets at the time and were not seriously injured. But we were terrified and could only scream,” she said.
